And Benny rolls a thirty-three on perception, which is excellent, and he sees the spiders before the spiders see him, and Josh gives them the chance to be stealthy. And this is where Johnny — I've got to hand it to Johnny, this was the play of the night, the Illusory Creature. He creates this big undead-looking thing, makes it look like it works for Grayson and the Necrolog folks—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's a nice touch, by the way. Using Grayson's aesthetic as the disguise. It's both a distraction and a — it's a little dig, right? It's Johnny being Johnny.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's perfect! And he has the illusion trip and get caught in the web and start screaming, and the performance check — he rolls a thirty-five on the performance check, which is a crit, and Josh lets it cover the whole group for stealth. And the diversion works, the spiders go swarming up toward the illusion, and the party sneaks across. It's clean, it's elegant, it's — I mean, this is what a bard is FOR, right? This is the bard fantasy.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'll give you this one. The illusory creature diversion was well-executed. The performance check was excellent. The stealth checks were — well, they were mixed. Argyle crit with a thirty-one, Johnny got a twenty-three with a mythic point, Anzu rolled a twenty, Benny got a twenty-seven. But Josh let the crit and the failure cancel out, so they all got through. And I think that ruling was—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Generous? Yeah, it was generous, but it was also — the crit and the failure canceling is a reasonable way to handle group checks, and the diversion was so good that it justified giving them the benefit of the doubt.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think it was more than generous. Benny's twenty-seven is a regular success. Johnny's twenty-three — on a mythic point, mind you — is a success. Anzu's twenty is a failure, Argyle's thirty-one is a crit. Josh had the crit cancel the failure, making it four regular successes. But by the letter, you'd want to look at whether Anzu's failure actually matters independently. In group stealth, it depends on how you run it. Josh ran it kindly. I'm not saying it's wrong, I'm saying it's kind.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's kind! And you know what, I'm fine with that, because they earned it with the diversion, and the scene was great, and then they get to the other side and they find — the shrine. The statues. And this is where the session goes from good dungeon crawl to genuinely significant lore drop.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Yes. This is the part that matters most, I think, and I want to make sure we get it right. They enter this chamber, and it's got stone — granite or marble — in a place where everything else is metal. The Strider is metal. The Undercroft is metal. And suddenly there's stone, and statues, and religious iconography. Argyle rolls a thirty-seven on religion.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: A thirty-seven! Which is —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is very high. And what he sees is six statues. Six figures. One in old Scale armor. One in the vestments of the Church of the Compelled from Raelion — which Johnny recognizes, and which Josh was clear no longer exists in any form. Two in Belvedere academic robes. One wearing clothes made of leaves and vines. And one — one very clearly in the vestments of the Iridescent Church, a face that everyone at the table would recognize: Aurelia the First.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Aurelia the First! The original Pontifex! And the six statues are her party — the group she led on her first crusade against the Dark Ages civilizations. And Josh drops this context, right, that each member of the party swore to a different outer god, and after the party broke up, they went their separate ways and formed their own religions and organizations. The Scale, Belvedere, the Iridescent Church — they all trace back to this original group.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which means this shrine is old. Anzu tries to date it with an academia check, gets a twenty-nine with Johnny's aid, and Josh tells them: probably minted before the time of Aurelia the Second, because that's when the church started separating its image from the other party members. Aurelia the Second was born one-oh-one AG. Current year is eight-sixty-three. So this shrine is roughly seven hundred years old, give or take.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Seven hundred years! In the Undercroft of the Strider! A shrine to all six outer gods, collectively, from before they split up! That's — I mean, that's a holy site, that's a pilgrimage site, and it's been — it's been webbed up and infested with spiders, and possibly co-opted by Big Bug. That's sacrilege on top of sacrilege, and it raises this enormous question: what IS the Strider? What's it built on? What's it built around?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's the question I think the table hasn't fully grappled with yet. They know the Undercroft is old. They know this shrine is old. They know the Fane down here mirrors the Strider. And now they know there's a shrine to all six outer gods collectively — which, as Josh noted, you don't see in the modern day, because the narrative doesn't support talking about how everyone used to be one big group. This is a pre-schism site. On the Strider. Under the Strider. Something the Strider was built on top of, or around, or—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Or the Strider IS the shrine, in some way, right? Like, maybe the Strider itself is — okay, I'm getting into speculation, I'll pull back, but the point is this is a massive lore beat and I don't think the table has fully processed it yet because they're too busy trying to survive.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which brings us to the combat.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The combat! Okay, so they're in the shrine, they're being stealthy, they can see the spiders moving around, and they decide — and this is where I think the argument about resource management really heats up — they decide to buff before engaging. They want to get off spells before combat starts. Argyle does Benediction, Johnny does Dirge of Doom, and they need to roll stealth to see if they get a second round of prep.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the stealth rolls are bad. Argyle gets a twenty-nine, which is good, but Anzu — I'm sorry, I need to check — actually, it was Argyle who got the twenty-nine, and someone got a sixteen.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The sixteen blew it. And Josh was clear: a twenty-nine is not good enough to save a sixteen. So the buff spells going off alerted the spiders, and combat starts. And here's my take: that's unlucky, but the decision to buff was correct. You want to go into a fight against unknown enemies with your auras up, especially when you can see they're large creatures with sword arms — sword arms, Maeve! Spiders with swords for front legs! That's — Josh said "their front two arms are swords" and everyone just lost it—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a horrifying image, yes. Giant spiders with blade-limbs. And the combat itself was — let me make sure I have the sequence right. Johnny goes first, casts Bless, then does a Distracting Performance to hide Benny. Rolls a thirty-eight on performance, which succeeds. Benny's hidden. Argyle goes, has Benediction and Bane running, raises his shield. Then the swarms act, shoot a web at Argyle, he barely makes the reflex save. Then Benny — Benny just goes off. Double slice, crit, sixty-two damage—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Sixty-two damage! Benny just — eviscerates them! And this is the thing about Benny, right, this is the nine-year-old android child just going absolutely nuclear on these spiders, and it's — you had to be there, honestly, just watching Mike roll dice and just go "kill kill kill kill"—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The "kill kill kill" was a highlight, yes. But I want to talk about the apothecary bug, because I think that's the real story of this combat.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The apothecary bug! Oh my god, the apothecary bug. Okay, so — so Johnny's standing there, he's been doing his bard thing, and suddenly this little spider — this little spider — jumps onto him and bites down. Josh makes Johnny roll a d-eight to determine which poison he gets. Johnny rolls a seven. And Josh says "no."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The d-eight determines which of several poisons the apothecary bug injects. Johnny rolled a seven, which was — it was just basic spider venom, I think, or something relatively mild. But then on the bug's next turn, it bites him again, and this time it's Sloughing Toxin, which — the description Josh gave was genuinely unsettling: your muscles start separating from your bones. Every time you take an action with the attack or move trait, you take poison damage.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Johnny's a bard! Everything he does has the attack or move trait! He's just — he's melting, he's melting while trying to fight, and then — THEN — the bug crawls into his bag and drinks his healing potion. It steals his healing potion! The apothecary bug has Potion Sight — which is apparently a real thing in Pathfinder Two-ee, Josh said "fun fact, the apothecary bug has potion sight, that's a real thing"—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It is a real ability. The apothecary bug can sense potions and will attempt to consume them, which destroys the potion and heals the bug. It's — I'll admit, it's a well-designed enemy for a party that carries a lot of consumables. It's just a nightmare for this specific group at this specific moment.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's a nightmare! And Johnny — Noah's reaction, just this mounting fury, "I hate this bug, this bug is my arch enemy" — and he means it! He means it with every fiber of his being! And the thing is, the bug keeps rolling well, and Johnny keeps — he tries Fear, he tries Inventive Vulnerability, he tries Bone Mow—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Bon mot.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Bon mot, right, bon mot, and the bug just — it doesn't care! It's immune to his BS! It's this little spider that just will not die and keeps poisoning him and stealing his stuff!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And then it gets worse, because the bug hits Johnny with Clown Monarch.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Clown Monarch! Which — okay, explain this to the audience, because this is—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Clown Monarch is a poison effect that, at stage one, causes you to fall prone and makes you roll a flat check to stand up. Your legs give out. So Johnny is on the ground, melting, poisoned, prone, and his legs won't work. And he just — stays down. He just lies there. "I'm not getting up."

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: "I'm not getting up." It's the funniest and saddest thing, because he's right! Why would he get up? Everything he does hurts him, the bug is on him, his legs don't work — just stay down, Johnny, just stay down and let the fighters handle it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And eventually they do. Argyle burns the bug off Johnny with Holy Light — literally puts a hand on the side of Johnny's head and blasts the bug — and then Anzu hits it with an Amped Telekinetic Projectile, and then Johnny — Johnny, on the ground, prone, poisoned — summons a Horde of Underlings, six tiny copies of himself that just swarm the bug, and then he stabs it with a dagger.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He stabs it with a dagger! He uses a mythic point to crit, and the bug has seven hit points left, seven, and Johnny's rolling two d-four, and everyone's just holding their breath, and — he kills it! He kills the bug! It's this beautiful, cathartic, ramshackle kill where everyone's just chipping away at this horrible little spider, and Johnny finally gets to be the one to put it down.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And then the bug explodes, leaving remnants of all its poisons spread across the floor.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Of course it does! Of course it explodes! It's the gift that keeps on giving! But — okay, here's where I want to come back to the resource argument, because by the time the bugs are dead, right, the party is hurting. Anzu caught Spider Venom from a crit — stage two, sickened two, clumsy one. Argyle got grabbed by webbing. Johnny's been through three different poisons. And their spell slots are just — gone. Argyle's burned all his fourths, most of his thirds. Anzu's down to scraps. Johnny's running on fumes.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: This is my point. This is exactly my point. They entered this combat already down a Fly and a Levitate from the piston room. They entered it after burning a Dimension Door. They entered it without having rested since the previous session's fights. And now they're at the bottom of unfamiliar stairs, in a Fane, in the Undercroft, with almost no spell slots left, multiple party members poisoned, and no safe place to rest.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they won! They won the fight! All the spiders are dead, the apothecary bug is dead, they're bloodied but standing—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Some of them are standing. Johnny was on the floor. Argyle had been grabbed. Anzu was sickened. And they're talking about resting right there in the shrine. In the spider-infested Fane. With no Rope Trick, no Leomund's Hut, no gingerbread house — which, by the way, Johnny sacrificed to a heart previously because he thought they wouldn't be doing a dungeon crawl. Two sessions later.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That is — okay, that is a funny and painful callback, I'll give you that. But the thing is, they don't have anywhere else to go. They can't make it back a quarter mile through webbed hallways. They can't rest in the piston room. The shrine is the best defensible position they've found. And Benny doesn't need to rest — Benny's a fighter, he's always at full capacity, he only took — what, eight points of damage all fight?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Benny is not the issue. Benny is never the issue. Benny is a nine-year-old android who does sixty-two damage on a crit and has no resources to exhaust. The issue is that their primary spellcasters are empty, their support is poisoned, and they haven't even found the heart yet. Josh ended the session with "we'll find out next time if there's a heart in this room, or perhaps in the room further up the stairs." They're at the foot of the stairs. They haven't reached the heart. They don't know what's protecting it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's the cliffhanger! That's a great cliffhanger! You're bloodied, you're depleted, you're standing in a seven-hundred-year-old shrine to six outer gods surrounded by spider corpses, and there are stairs going up, and you don't know what's at the top. That's — that's perfect dungeon crawl pacing, Maeve, that's exactly the tension you want.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's perfect pacing if they survive next session. If they go up those stairs with no spells and fight something with a heart — something that can co-opt a Fane, something that can coerce a heart into serving it — and they TPK, then this session is the session where they made the wrong call. And I think they know it. I think you can hear it in the table chatter at the end, where they're all going "there's no way there's a bigger spider" and Josh is just laughing.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Josh's laugh! Josh's laugh at the end was — it was malevolent, it was pure GM energy, just this—"that would be terrible if there was a big spider in this area with spiders in it, that would be crazy"—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He's not even hiding it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He's not hiding it! But — okay, here's my counterpoint. Even if there IS something at the top of those stairs, right, even if there's a boss, the party has options. They can rest. They can take ten minutes, patch up wounds — Argyle has Treat Wounds, he did it during the fight, patched Johnny up between rounds. They can recover some HP, maybe recover from the poisons. They're not at zero, they're at low.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They can't recover spell slots from a ten-minute rest. They need a full night. And they have no safe place to take one. That's the squeeze.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's the squeeze, and I think — look, I think that's intentional. I think Josh has been building toward this. He said it himself at the end: "I've made you too complacent. You haven't been in areas long enough where you might have to rest with enemies nearby, so no one has any spells for doing that." He knows. He designed this. He put them in a position where their usual tools don't work, where they can't just pop a hut and sleep safe, and that's — that's good GMing. That's challenging your players.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's good GMing if the challenge is fair. It's good GMing if there's a path through that doesn't require resources they don't have. We don't know that yet. We'll find out next session.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: We'll find out next session. But — can I just — before we wrap, can I just say one more thing about the apothecary bug fight? Because I think there's a real design question here, and I want to hear your take. The apothecary bug — is it a fair enemy? Is it a fair enemy to put against a party that's already depleted, that's already in a Fane, that's already dealing with sword-spiders? Because the potion stealing, the multiple poisons, the d-eight random poison table — that's a lot of mechanics on one little creature.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a lot, but it's — the apothecary bug is a real bestiary creature, Josh confirmed that. He said "this is a real guy." The potion sight, the random poisons, the sloughing toxin, the clown monarch — those are all real abilities. It's not a Josh invention. It's a real creature that he placed appropriately in an environment where it makes sense. It's a creature that lives in dark places, that feeds on potions, that uses poisons. It belongs in the Undercroft. It belongs in a spider-infested Fane. I think it's fair.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Even the potion stealing? Even crawling into Johnny's bag and drinking his healing potion?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Especially the potion stealing. That's the creature's whole thing. It's an apothecary bug — it steals potions. That's what it does. If you don't want it to steal your potions, kill it before it gets to your bag. They didn't, because they were dealing with the sword-spiders first, which was the correct tactical priority — the sword-spiders were doing more damage — but the consequence of that priority is the bug gets to your consumables. That's a tradeoff, not a gimmick.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I — okay, I actually think you're right about that. I think the apothecary bug is fair. I think it's brutal, and I think Johnny will have nightmares about it for weeks, but it's fair. It's a creature doing what it does, and the party made choices that let it do its thing.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Johnny will never forget the apothecary bug. Johnny will be talking about the apothecary bug in season five.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Johnny will be writing poems about the apothecary bug. Bad poems. Angry poems. It's going to be — honestly, it's going to be great content. But — okay, final thought. The shrine. The statues. Aurelia's party. I think this is the thing that's going to matter most, long-term. Not the combat, not the resource drain, not the apothecary bug — the shrine. Because if the Strider is built on a seven-hundred-year-old site of worship to all six outer gods, and if that site has been co-opted by something, by Big Bug or whatever's up those stairs, then the whole pilgrimage — the whole thing they're on, the nineteen orgs, the tithe, the Harlequin, all of it — it's built on top of something much older and much stranger than any of them realize.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think you're right about that. And I think the question of whether the heart down here is still serving the Strider or serving something else is the question that will define the back half of this arc. If they kill the heart and the Fane collapses — if the structure collapses with it, because the Fane is grafted onto existing structure — they could damage the Strider itself. That's a risk they haven't talked about.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: They haven't! And that's — okay, that's actually a great point, because Josh was clear: when a Fane is grafted onto existing structure, killing the heart removes the Fane qualities but the structure remains. But if the structure IS the Strider — if the Fane is woven into the Strider's own machinery — then killing the heart might not collapse the building, but it might change what the building does. It might change the Strider.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or it might free the Strider from whatever's coercing its heart. If Big Bug is co-opting a heart that's supposed to serve the Strider, killing Big Bug and freeing the heart might be the best thing they could do for the pilgrimage.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Or it might make the Strider stop working entirely, and then all nineteen orgs are stranded in the void with no way to reach the wall. That's — that's a real choice, right? That's a real dilemma. Do you kill the heart and risk the Strider, or do you leave it and risk whatever Big Bug is doing with it?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's the dilemma, and they're going to have to face it next session with no spell slots and no safe rest. So.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So it's going to be great. It's going to be a disaster and it's going to be great. Happy birthday to Tanner, I guess.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Josh said he can't kill Anzu because it'd be too rude right before his birthday. I'm sure that restraint will last exactly until the first roll next session.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It absolutely will not. He's going to open next session with a lich that steals experience points.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He literally threatened that. He literally said "I'm going to make you fight an A-D-and-D lich that can take levels from you as one of its attacks."

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then he realized they're on milestone leveling so it wouldn't work, and you could just — you could hear the disappointment. He was so upset. He really wanted that lich.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He really did. God help them when he figures out a workaround.

episodes.title: The Heart in the Basement

A.name: Bram
A.persona: warm, boisterous, fluent but imprecise; the storyteller who relives the best moments with relish and happily embellishes. Talks in long, rolling run-on sentences that pile clause on clause; makes big sweeping claims he then has to walk back; reliably gets a name, number, or detail wrong and gets corrected (usually by Maeve); now and then runs clean out of sentence and lands on a shrug like "you... you had to be there." Drives the recap forward and overshoots

B.name: Maeve
B.persona: warm and dry, precise but pointed; the long-time regular whose knowledge of the setting is lived rather than studied. Lands the exact word, name, or date the others fumble for and reins Bram in with a flat one-line correction — she finishes her sentences and finishes them short. But she's not only the fact-checker: she needles, too, pushing on WHY the characters did what they did and making Bram defend his reads, poking at the table's heroics and at sentiment with a wink. Grounds events in how the world actually works; the only one reliably right, so let her be plainly wrong exactly once so she isn't an oracle

episodes.synopsis: Deep within an ancient, forgotten section of the Strider, the party licks their wounds among statues of the first Aurelia's original adventuring company. Pressing onward, they discover a vast chamber housing a colossal mechanical heart — the Strider's own lifeblood — guarded by conduit nodes, swarming hivelings, and a cunning spider known as Vrax'leth that travels through the pipes. After a grueling battle of shattered tubes and evaded death-rays, the party frees the heart and awakens something ancient: the Machine God, an old heart from the era of Aurelia I, long enslaved by the false god Herald. A deal is struck — purge the Strider of Herald's remaining followers, and earn a powerful new ally.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay so look, the big moment of the night — the thing everyone's going to be talking about — is obviously the Machine God. You cannot tell me that wasn't one of the all-time great reveals in this campaign, because here they are, right, they're sitting in this ancient forgotten basement of the Strider, they're surrounded by these beautiful seven-hundred-year-old statues of Aurelia the First's original adventuring company, and they have no idea — no idea — that they're about to stumble into what is essentially a sleeping deity, a heart from the era when hearts were actually worshipped as gods, and it just — it wakes up and talks to them in this grinding metal voice and says "little one, I have not spoken to one in a very long time," and I mean come on, that's — that's movie stuff, that's the kind of moment you remember for years.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a good reveal. I'll give you that. But can we back up? Because the reason they got there at all is a decision I want to talk about first — they pushed forward into the room with barely any resources, half of them diseased, Argyle's sitting on exactly two fourth-level spell slots, and Anzu just says "we're not going to rest, right? We're just going right in?"

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And they were right to push! They'd just cleared the spider room, they'd cleared the piston room, the momentum was there, and sometimes — look, sometimes the table knows, right, you can feel it, the energy is building and you just — you go. You don't stop and rest in a spider-infested basement because you're tired. You push through.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They literally stopped and rested. That's what happened next. They made a lean-to out of fallen masonry and slept in a corner.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, fine, fine, but the point is they didn't go back. They didn't retreat to the surface. They rested in the room and then pushed forward, and that push-forward is what got them to the Machine God. If they'd gone back to Iconoclasm, if they'd said oh let's rest somewhere safe, they never find this thing.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or they find it at full strength and the fight goes completely differently. We'll come back to that. But I want to start with the rest itself, because I think it matters. Johnny is carrying Avernal Fever from two sessions ago — a disease he never got cured because Argyle doesn't prepare Cleanse Affliction and won't until next level. That's a table management problem.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's a Pathfinder problem, more than a table problem. The spell tax on disease removal in this edition is brutal — you need a fourth-rank slot for a level-appropriate disease, and Argyle's got more pressing things to prepare. He's got heals, he's got Spiritual Weapon, he's got — look, he's the only healer in the party, he can't afford to blow a top-rank slot on "Johnny feels a little warm."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Avernal Fever isn't "a little warm." It's an infernal disease. And Johnny fails Fortitude saves against everything gross — Josh basically confirmed it at the table, the man has no immune system, which is darkly funny for a character who literally resurrects from death, but it's also a real liability. Argyle finally remembered he could Treat Disease during the rest, which is what saved Johnny, but that took them an embarrassing amount of table time to figure out.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they figured it out! And this is what I love about this group, right, they're not optimized, they're not — they don't sit down with spreadsheets, they just kind of muddle through, and the muddling is what makes it feel real. Argyle treating Johnny's disease while they're huddled under a stone lean-to in a seven-hundred-year-old room surrounded by statues of dead heroes — that's a scene. That's atmosphere.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The statues are a good scene, I agree. And the Argyle connection is genuinely interesting — he walks up to the statue of Coulombe Honorsworn, the founder of the Scale, and Josh tells him the face looks familiar, there's a familial resemblance to his grandmother. That's not nothing. That's a thread.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's huge! Argyle is — okay, so Argyle is a former celestial and a former devil sharing a body, right, and now he's just the celestial half with a custode from the Scale on loan to Iconoclasm, and he's standing in front of the literal founder of his organization, carved in stone, in a room that's been sealed for centuries, and there's a connection to his family line? That's — you can't tell me that's not going to pay off later. That's Chekhov's statue.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Maybe. Or maybe it's just flavor text. Josh does that — he seeds things that feel loaded and sometimes they're just texture. I'm more interested in what happened during Anzu's watch, because that's where the session's real tension starts.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The sounds! Yes! So Anzu takes first watch, rolls a perception check, and Josh gives him this incredible description — he can hear, beneath the regular mechanical thrum of the Strider, something irregular. Something moving with intent. These metal-on-metal raps, pauses, then it picks up again, and it's not getting closer, it's just... there. For the entire four hours.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And then Benny takes over and rolls lower and can't hear it at all. Which is — look, I know Josh said maybe it got quieter, but I think that's the Vrax'leth setup. The spider's in there, doing something, and Anzu caught it and Benny didn't. That's a genuine tactical miss. If Benny had heard it, they might have gone in more carefully.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they went in loud anyway! That's the thing — Johnny's casting Dirge of Doom and Bless and Haste before they even cross the threshold, Josh explicitly tells them "you're announcing your entrance," and they just... go. No stealth. No subtlety. Just four guys with music playing walking into a room they've never seen.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Because Anzu's scouting was incomplete. Othello flew in, got a look around — saw the four vats with runes floating in red liquid, the mechanical ball on a cart in the center, and the giant half-torso mecha at the back — but rolled poorly on perception. Anzu even said it himself, he got "a pretty bad check," and then he and the table kind of talked themselves into believing there was nothing alive in there.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: To be fair, the room was empty of visible creatures. The spider was inside the pipes. That's — Vrax'leth was hiding in the conduit system, right, it's this little blue-purple-yellow spider that floats through the liquid in the vats and travels through the pipes, and it had readied an attack for when they entered. That's a smart enemy. That's a GM who designed a boss around its environment.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And I want to talk about the augury, because I think that's where the table talked themselves into a bad call. Argyle casts Augury asking "would it be bad if we break this heart," and Josh gives him a good feeling. But Argyle's asking about breaking the heart — the heart they haven't even met yet. He doesn't know it's the Machine God. He doesn't know it's sentient. He doesn't know it's an ally. He's asking "should we destroy this thing for energy" and the spell says "yeah, go ahead."

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's — okay, I see where you're going, but I think you're wrong here. The Augury is asking about the outcome of a course of action, right, and the outcome of breaking the heart is — well, it turns out the Machine God himself says he'd be fine with them taking a piece of him. He offers them a piece voluntarily. So the Augury was correct. Breaking the heart wouldn't have been catastrophic.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But it would have killed a potential ally worth far more than two hundred energy. The Augury told them "no bad effects" and they took that as "this is safe to do." If they'd rolled poorly on that diplomacy check with the Machine God — and Johnny hit a nat twenty, which is the only reason any of this worked — they might have just killed it for the energy and never known what they lost.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — okay, that's a fair point, the nat twenty on the diplomacy check is doing a lot of work here. But I think you're underrating how the scene played out emotionally, because even without the dice, right, even if Johnny rolls average, the party's choice to kneel down and talk to this thing instead of just smashing it — that's character. That's who they are. Johnny says "are you okay? There was a spider in you." That's —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's a very Johnny line, yes.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's perfect! It's this bard who's been getting poisoned and diseased all session, who's been screaming about apothecary bugs, and he kneels down in front of an ancient mechanical god and goes "hey buddy, you doing alright?" That's the heart of the table right there.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'll concede the characterization. But let's talk about the fight itself, because I think the conduit node mechanic was the most interesting encounter design Josh has done all season, and I think the party played it sloppily.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Sloppily! They won!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They won because Benny's damage output is absurd and because Johnny finally landed some crits on the hivelings. But the strategy was a mess. You've got four conduit nodes, each one does something different — one fires a death ray that does massive electric damage to a marked square, one shoots webs that grab you, one spawns hivelings, one does a mental fear effect — and the party doesn't know which is which for most of the fight. They're just hitting whatever's closest.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But that's the encounter! You're supposed to learn by doing. The first time the death ray fires, it evaporates a hiveling instantly — forty-five electric damage to anything in the square — and the party goes "oh, we need to not stand there." Then Argyle immediately starts thinking about whether they can bait it onto the nodes. That's reactive tactics. That's reading the room.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Except they never actually executed on it. Argyle yells "we can cluster around the conduit nodes to get it to hit them" but then nobody does it. The death ray keeps firing on empty squares or on hivelings, and the party just kills the nodes one by one with raw damage.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which worked!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which worked because Benny can crit for over a hundred damage on a tube of glass with a butterfly sword. That's not strategy, that's a damage check.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, but the Vrax'leth thing — the actual spider, the heart thief — that's the clever part of the encounter. It's not just sitting there taking hits. It's traveling through the pipes. It pops out of one tube, attacks, goes back in, moves to another tube. It's whack-a-mole. You have to destroy the tubes to corner it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And they failed to corner it! Vrax'leth escaped. Johnny summoned eight underlings to box it in — which was genuinely clever, by the way, using the summon spell as a containment tool rather than a damage tool — but the spider just tumbles through them, because the underlings automatically fail all saving throws, and it disappears into the central orb. Then Benny smashes the orb, a dead spider pops out, and... that's it. It's dead. But they didn't kill it through strategy. They killed it because it was inside the thing they were already smashing.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: A kill's a kill! And I would argue that destroying all the conduits and the central orb was the strategy — they systematically took away every place the spider could hide until the only place left was the one they were breaking. That's cornering, even if it doesn't look like a chess move.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'd buy that if they'd done it intentionally. But the sequence was: Benny smashes Beta, spider doesn't pop out. Benny smashes the central orb later, dead spider pops out. They didn't know the spider was in there. They got lucky.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Fine, fine, there's luck involved. There's always luck involved. But I want to talk about what I think was the real tactical story of this fight, which is Argyle getting webbed — how many times was it, four? Five?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: At least four. Beta's web attack targeted Argyle repeatedly.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Argyle just — he takes it. He's stuck there, he can't move, he's spending actions trying to escape, and the whole time he's saying "it's fine, it's fine, if it keeps webbing me it's not webbing you guys." He's being a damage sponge. He's being a tank. That's the champion's job.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's a very generous reading. I think Argyle got webbed because he was in a bad position and couldn't get out, not because he was sacrificing himself. He even said at one point, quote, I'm very fine getting spiderwebbed repeatedly if it lets you guys bash things, end quote — but that's rationalizing after the fact. He was stuck. His Spiritual Weapon kept missing. He tried Percussive Impact and missed. He had — what was it — three or four rounds where he did almost nothing useful.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But he kept casting! He kept sustaining Spiritual Weapon, he kept healing, he burned the webs with Holy Light — which was a good call, by the way, clearing the web tiles so they couldn't hide hivelings —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That was a good call, I'll give you that. Burning the web thicket was smart. But his damage output was negligible. The nodes went down to Benny and Anzu, not to Argyle.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's — okay, that's fair, but Argyle's not a damage dealer, he's a champion. His job is battlefield control and support. The Holy Light burn, the Battle Medicine on Benny that critted and gave him a mythic point back, the Divine Wrath that vaporized a hiveling on a crit fail — he was doing his job. He was the glue.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Divine Wrath was good. I'll give you the Divine Wrath. But let's talk about Anzu's fight, because I think Anzu had a worse round than Argyle, and I don't think the table's talking about it enough.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Anzu had a rough fight, no question. He got grabbed by the web attack early, spent his whole first turn escaping, then got grabbed again later, and then he was stupefied on top of it, so he's making flat checks just to cast cantrips —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He failed both flat checks on one turn. He was immobilized and stupefied, he needed to pass a DC five check for the grab and a DC six for the stupefied, and he couldn't do either. His entire turn was gone. And then on a later turn he burned his last focus point on an Amped Telekinetic Projectile and missed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But when he did hit — when he hit the conduit node with the telekinetic projectile for thirty-four damage — that was the one that shattered it. That was a big moment. And the bludgeoning weakness on the nodes meant his telekinetic projectile was actually one of the most efficient damage sources they had. Once he recalled knowledge and learned the weakness, he was calling it out — quote, bludgeoning damage, everybody, end quote. That's the psychic being useful in a knowledge way even when his spells are getting shut down.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The recall knowledge was good. Learning the bludgeoning weakness — and the fact that the nodes are immune to spirit damage, which Argyle should have known before he wasted Spiritual Weapon on one — that was the turning point. But Anzu's performance overall was rough. He spent more actions escaping webs than doing anything productive.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The fight was rough for everybody except Benny. Let's just acknowledge — Benny was the MVP of this encounter, hands down. The double slice on the conduit node, the crit with the butterfly sword, the switch to the polytool for bludgeoning damage once they learned the weakness — I mean, Benny's switching his weapon's damage type on the fly to exploit a weakness he just learned about, that's —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's good tactical play, yes. The polytool shift to bludgeoning was the single smartest moment of the fight. And his damage numbers were genuinely ridiculous. He hit Beta for over a hundred damage in one turn.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Over a hundred! On a tube of glass!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: On a tube with hardness, no less. The butterfly sword is doing too much damage for a two-d-four weapon.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's the twinned weapon property, right, the stacking damage, plus the spirit damage, plus — look, Benny's a fighter, fighters hit things, that's what they do. And Mike plays Benny with this beautiful energy where he's just — he's this nine-year-old android child who is also a killing machine, and he's foaming at the mouth because the spider finally hit him. Quote, now he has a reason to kill these. Before, he didn't really know. He was like, I don't know, maybe they're mean or something, end quote.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That was a great line, I'll admit. Benny's characterization carries encounters.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then Johnny — poor Johnny, right — Johnny spends most of this fight running after Benny trying to keep buffs up, his Dirge of Doom keeps getting mentioned and then not mattering because the hivelings are trivial, and he keeps trying to cast things on the central orb and getting told quote, it's not a creature, it doesn't have a mind, end quote. He tries Invented Vulnerability on a conduit node — immune to mental. He tries Albatross Curse on the orb — that targets a creature. He literally starts reciting the Rime of the Ancient Mariner at a ball and then gives up and throws needle darts at it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the needle darts did fifteen damage, which was enough to start cracks in the orb. So Johnny's damage, even when he's fumbling, is contributing. And his Invented Vulnerability on Vrax'leth itself was huge — five slashing weakness, then eight underlings at fourth rank doing eight-d-four plus forty damage. That bloodied the spider.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Eighty-four damage! From Johnny! The bard who keeps failing fortitude saves! And then — the moment — the conduit reforms. The glass around Beta rebuilds itself because the spider's been bloodied and it triggers some kind of regeneration. Josh literally takes the dead condition off the conduit. The tube came back from the dead.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That was cruel. That was genuinely cruel encounter design. You smash a tube, you think it's gone, and then the act of bloodying the boss brings it back. That's a gut punch.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But it's fair! It's telegraphed — the room shakes every time they break a tube, right, the heart is reacting. The healing is coming from the heart. It makes sense that the system would try to repair itself.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It makes sense, but it also means the encounter is a damage race in a way that punishes the party for having already spent most of their resources in the previous two rooms. If they'd come in fresh, the conduits reforming wouldn't matter — they'd have the spell slots to burn through it. Coming in depleted, it nearly killed them.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But it didn't! And that's — look, we keep coming back to this, they were depleted and they went in anyway and they won. Sometimes the gamble pays off.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Sometimes the gamble pays off. I want that on record. Because next time it might not.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Noted. Can we talk about the Machine God now? Because this is — this is the thing. This is the moment.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Let's talk about it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So they clear the room, Vrax'leth is dead, the conduits are shattered, and Johnny — Johnny just walks up to this giant mechanical half-torso with a glowing orb in its chest and says hello. And Josh has him roll diplomacy. Nat twenty. Natural freaking twenty.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the Machine God responds. In this grinding, metal-on-metal voice. Quote, little one, I have not spoken to one in a very long time, end quote. And you can feel — I mean, Josh's delivery on this was —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It was incredible. And the lore dump! So Argyle rolls a religion check, gets a thirty-eight after Johnny's aid bumps him up, and Josh lays out this whole history: in the early days of Aurelia the First, hearts were believed to be gods manifest on Færrin. They were treated as deities. Then after Aurelia the Second, the manufacturing process changed, hearts became less powerful, and the church declared that modern hearts aren't direct divine manifestations. But the old ones — the old ones are different. They have abilities modern hearts don't. And this is one of them.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Argyle would know this because he's interacted with an old heart before — Voice of Many, the one that could make large jumps across the Infinite Horizon. So he has context for what they're looking at. This isn't just a stronger version of their little Eerie heart back at base. This is something from a different era entirely.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And the Machine God confirms it, right — he was Aurelia's eyes and ears. He worked with the original party. He's been trapped in this Strider, adrift on the horizon, for centuries. The Strider was a trap that was never sprung. His inhabitants were taken and changed by Herald —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The false god. One of the outer gods, or something claiming to be one. The Machine God calls it quote, a false god, one of many, worming its way into the people for years, centuries, end quote. And Johnny immediately connects the dots — quote, was its name Herald? end quote

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which is — that's a callback to earlier in the season, right, the whole Strider pilgrimage is voidward, toward the wall, and the theory from Kadou was that Raelion was thrown voidward past the wall and the Voidsong is its cry for help. And now we've got an ancient heart saying Herald's followers are on this ship, they wormed their way in, they have a destination in mind. That's — those threads are converging.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They are. And I think the most important detail the Machine God gives them is about the followers. There are — well, there were three groups, now two since they killed Vrax'leth's spiders. One is dormant, would activate at the right conditions — presumably when the Strider reaches whatever destination Herald's followers are aiming for. The other is active, growing, on the other side of the Strider, and has recently taken on new members from outside and is converting people from inside.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's where Anzu's sister is.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's the implication, yes. Anzu's been trying to reach his sister, who's somewhere on the Strider, and now the Machine God is telling them there's an active cult of Herald on that side of the ship. That's personal stakes for Anzu.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Argyle immediately goes — quote, I got resurrect now, so if we gotta kill her, we can bring her back, end quote. Which is — okay, that's dark, but it's also practical, and it's very Argyle. He's thinking about the mission. But the table's reaction, right, Benny's like quote, we going to kill her right, guys? end quote and it's this moment of — are they actually considering killing Anzu's sister if she's been converted?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think that's a real question this table is going to have to answer. The Machine God's deal is clear: purge Herald's remaining followers from the Strider, and it lends them its support. That's the quest. And if Anzu's sister is among the converted, that's a moral dilemma this table hasn't faced before.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But that's next session. That's — we're not there yet. What I want to talk about is the deal itself, because I think the party made the right call. They didn't kill the heart for two hundred energy. They didn't harvest it. They struck an alliance.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I agree that keeping the Machine God alive was the right call, but I want to push on why. The two hundred energy is a lot — it's more than they've gotten from any single source this season. But the Machine God offers something energy can't buy: eyes and ears throughout the Strider. It can see everything inside its own body. It knows where the Herald cultists are. It can communicate with them telepathically without a totem. And it's an old heart with unknown capabilities that dwarf anything modern hearts can do.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So the calculus is obvious — two hundred energy now, or a living ally that can see the whole board.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Right. But here's what I want to push on: Argyle asks if the Machine God would connect to the tithe system, and the Machine God says it's loathe to connect itself to quote, whatever infernal machinery has been added to the Strider, end quote, but would do so if necessary for their survival. And Argyle immediately says quote, don't do it yet, this is a last resort, end quote. Which I think is correct, but also — that's a contingency plan. That's the party's emergency button if the tithe becomes unsustainable. And I don't think they're fully thinking through what it means to have an ancient heart plugged into the tithe network.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The tithe drains energy from hearts. If they connect the Machine God to the tithe, it's being drained alongside everyone else. But it's also an enormously powerful old heart — does it have enough energy to sustain the tithe where others don't? Could it replace Obratz as the energy source that keeps the Strider running? And if so, what does that mean for the faction politics on the surface? If the Machine God is secretly paying the tithe, the surface factions don't need to fight over energy anymore, which means the party's whole alliance structure becomes irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — okay, that's a big swing. I think you're getting ahead of the table. Right now they've got a quest — kill two more cult groups, earn an ally. That's clear, that's actionable, and that's what they're going to do next session.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Probably. But Argyle also mentioned wanting to use a Ring of Truth on everyone in their alliance next session to root out spies, which — given that the Machine God already told them none of their allies inside the Strider are actively screwing them over — might be unnecessary. And might offend people.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But the Machine God said it can't see above the Strider. It only sees inside. The allies who might be compromised — Tas from Prime Meridian, Hildebrandt — their dealings could be happening on the surface where the Machine God can't see.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's a fair distinction. The Machine God's knowledge is limited to the interior. But still — walking into your alliance meeting and going everyone drink this truth serum is not a diplomacy move.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's a very Argyle move, though.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It is. It is a very Argyle move.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Can we talk about the loot, at least? Because the Machine God gives them a piece of itself — a Greater Jolt Coil, spellheart, electric resistance and lightning bolt — and the Vrax'leth corpse, which can be fashioned into a Usurper's Crown, plus one to mental saves, once per day turn a failed mental save into a success.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The crown's the better item. Five hundred gold value, and the mental save turnaround is exactly what this party needs — they just spent an entire fight getting feared by a conduit node's mental attack. Anzu was stupefied, half the party was frightened. Mental protection is their weak spot.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Anzu couldn't identify it. He rolled a twenty-three on the occultism check, which was a failure. So they're sitting on a dead spider they can't fully assess until they rest and retry.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Josh ended up just giving it to them, which — I mean, I understand, it was the end of the session and the stakes were low, but that's the second time Josh has handed them information they didn't earn because the session was running long. I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's pragmatic. You don't want to end a session on you can't identify the loot, see you next week. That's an anticlimax.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You identify it next session. That's how it works.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Not everyone is as patient as you. Some of us want to know if we're wearing a dead spider on our head.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You're wearing a dead spider on your head.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The Usurper's Crown! It's a crown made from a spider's cephalothorax! That's metal as hell!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It is admittedly metal. Both senses.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then — the level-up. They hit level eight. Argyle's already got his sheet sent to Josh, which Josh is both annoyed and delighted by. Anzu's got new spells to pick. And the table ends on this naming discussion, which has been going on for multiple sessions now — they've gone through Chronicle, Heartbreakers, Choir, Topside Boys, and now Argyle proposes the Coalition.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Coalition is fine. It's not exciting, but it's fine. Benny still wants to be the Heartbreakers secretly, which is the best idea anyone's had.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Heartbreakers is great! Heartbreakers is — it's got edge, it's got humor, it references what they actually do, which is break hearts —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It references what they do, yes. The Coalition sounds like a government agency.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But that's the point! Argyle says it himself — they like simple, generic names. The Wayfinders, the adventurers. They're not trying to be cool, they're trying to be functional. And the Coalition with a Ki-Rin on the flag is — okay, the Ki-Rin thing is weird because they killed Ki-Rin, like, that's a trophy from a fight, but —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They killed corrupted Ki-Rin. The Ki-Rin itself is presumably a noble creature. Having it on your flag is a statement about what you're fighting for, not what you killed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Exactly! It's aspirational. It's — look, the naming thing is going to keep going, it's going to be next session too, and I don't think we need to resolve it here. What I want to say is — this was a session where the table went in tired, went in depleted, went in with diseases and missing spell slots, and they came out with a new ally that fundamentally changes the strategic landscape of the entire Strider arc. They came out with a quest that has personal stakes for Anzu. They came out with loot that patches their biggest defensive weakness. And they leveled up. That's a session.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'll give you most of that. I think the fight was messier than it needed to be, I think they got bailed out by a nat twenty on the diplomacy check, and I think the augury was a misuse of a spell that could have gone very badly. But the outcome — the Machine God, the quest, the lore — I can't argue with the outcome. It's the biggest thing that's happened this season.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Bigger than the tithe? Bigger than Obratz getting wrung dry on the dance floor?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The tithe was the inciting incident. The Machine God is the pivot. Everything after this is about Herald, about the voidward journey, about what's waiting at the wall. The tithe told them they were in danger. The Machine God tells them what the danger is for.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — yeah. That's a good way to put it. The Strider isn't just a ship. It's a trap. It's a vessel that was taken over by a false god's followers, and the party is now inside it, making deals with the thing that used to run it. That's — that's the season, right there. That's the whole season in one image.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And next session they either go after the active cult on the other side of the Strider — where Anzu's sister probably is — or they try to deal with the dormant one first. Or they go back to the surface and try to manage their alliances with the Ring of Truth idea. They've got options.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Too many options. That's their problem. They always have too many options and not enough spell slots.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Some things don't change with level.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Ha. No, they don't. But you know what does change? Now they've got a Machine God in their corner. And I cannot wait to see what that looks like when the Herald cultists find out.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Assuming the cultists don't find out first. The Machine God just joined their skein network — everyone in the alliance can see it now. Machine God has joined the chat, all caps, different font. That's not subtle.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No. No, it is not. And that's going to be a problem.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's going to be a problem.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Next Monday.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Next Monday.

episodes.title: The Checkout Card and the Bone Dragon
episodes.episodeTitle: The Checkout Card and the Bone Dragon

A.name: Bram
A.persona: warm, boisterous, fluent but imprecise; the storyteller who relives the best moments with relish and happily embellishes. Talks in long, rolling run-on sentences that pile clause on clause; makes big sweeping claims he then has to walk back; reliably gets a name, number, or detail wrong and gets corrected (usually by Maeve); now and then runs clean out of sentence and lands on a shrug like "you... you had to be there." Drives the recap forward and overshoots

B.name: Maeve
B.persona: warm and dry, precise but pointed; the long-time regular whose knowledge of the setting is lived rather than studied. Lands the exact word, name, or date the others fumble for and reins Bram in with a flat one-line correction — she finishes her sentences and finishes them short. But she's not only the fact-checker: she needles, too, pushing on WHY the characters did what they did and making Bram defend his reads, poking at the table's heroics and at sentiment with a wink. Grounds events in how the world actually works; the only one reliably right, so let her be plainly wrong exactly once so she isn't an oracle

episodes.synopsis: Fresh from their alliance with the machine god in the Undercroft, the party returns to the surface to settle accounts with the skeletal librarian Ocelith, trading a mysterious ink ribbon for a colossal Void Atlas that charts the horizon ahead. With Kadou's help, they study the atlas and identify tantalizing destinations on the horizon, including the legendary moving city of the Menagerie. Back at base, the coalition's loyalties are put to the test with a Ring of Truth ceremony, the party successfully recruits the gun-toting Radiant Arms to consolidate their defenses, and debates how best to fortify their strider heart against rival factions lurking nearby.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, no, no, no — you can't tell me that the funniest thing that happened all night wasn't Mike literally typing "how do I kill Anzu" into the optimization bot and getting a step-by-step murder guide back, complete with a little sassy attitude from the AI about how maybe you shouldn't be doing this, and it's like, buddy, you don't know these people, this is the most normal Tuesday for them.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: What I want to know is why Tanner was upset about the GM learning Anzu's a glass cannon when the entire table was watching Mike feed his stats into a bot specifically to find the fastest kill combo against a party member. The GM didn't need the bot to figure out the psychic with the low fortitude is squishy.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — okay, that's fair, but you're missing the spirit of the thing, which is that it was deeply, hilariously on-brand for Benny to be like, "yes, I would like to optimize my child soldier's damage output against my ally, thank you," and the bot coming back with like, "I don't know if you should be doing this," like a little digital conscience that immediately got ignored.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The bot had more moral hesitation than the party. That tracks.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It really does! But okay, let's actually get into the session, because the real meat of this one starts when they're back with the Machine God, right, and Argyle — and this is the thing I loved — Argyle immediately goes, hey, can you defend yourself better now, can you hide, because he's thinking about operational security for this ancient heart they just befriended, which I thought was a really smart instinct.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It was a smart instinct, yes. What was less smart was immediately asking for group telepathy and not thinking for even one second about the fact that the Machine God can hear everything they say to each other. Josh basically told them to their faces — whatever you communicate with each other, the Machine God can also hear it. And nobody blinked.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Because they don't care! They didn't care last campaign either, they used to split chats and take turns in different channels, and the entity on the other end still heard everything. This is a party that has made peace with the concept of a cosmic eavesdropper. And honestly? The Machine God is an ancient heart from Aurelia the First's era. He's been around for seven hundred years. He's not going to betray them over group chat gossip about where to put turrets.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You don't know that. You don't know what an ancient mechanical heart's priorities are. They've known this entity for what, one conversation? And they've already handed him their entire communication network. Every plan, every secret, every strategy discussion now flows through a being they met because they smashed his tubes and killed his spider.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: They killed the spider that was parasitizing him! That's like saying you can't trust the doctor because you killed the tumor. The Machine God was grateful, he gave them the Jolt Coil, he gave them Vrax'leth's corpse for the crown, he connected to their heart network — this is an alliance, Maeve, not a hostage situation.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Fine. Let's move to the library, then, because if you want to talk about trust and risk, the Ocelith scene is where I actually have problems.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the ink ribbon trade! Yes! So they go back to the library, they hand Ocelith his precious ink ribbon — which they never identified, by the way, they just grabbed it and went, "here you go, mystery item, hope it's not nuclear launch codes," which Argyle literally said, and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He said that after handing it over. The sequence matters. They walked in, gave the skeletal dragon-armadillo librarian his stolen ribbon, and he slots it into a typewriter. A typewriter. On his desk. And then he pulls out this massive atlas, and instead of just giving it to them, he asks them to sign a checkout card. An index card in the front cover of the book. With a ballpoint pen. And Anzu signs his real name.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, the real name thing — look, in the moment, I get it, you're standing in front of a giant bone dragon who's being polite and you've just completed a fetch quest, you're not in a paranoia headspace. And Argyle did try to check the signatures, he rolled terribly, couldn't recognize anyone —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He rolled a natural one. And then Anzu inspects the pen, finds nothing magical about it, inspects the index card, gets a faint whiff of magic but can't identify what it does, and signs anyway. With his real name. The scion of the Qureshi family, a runaway from Belvedere aristocracy, puts his actual signature on a magical card he can't identify, in a library run by a skeletal dragon who tells him — and I want you to really sit with this — "books always come back to this library. They always do."

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's just a librarian being a librarian! The man loves his collection!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The man is a nine-foot-tall bone dragon who smelled the ribbon like he had a nose, which he doesn't, and then smiled about it. And the previous person to check out this book was Alastair Moss, who Anzu later identifies as someone from Pyrolyte. Specifically from Project Entrainment — the project that sends people to the Source of the Voidsong. Six months ago. So a person connected to void experimentation had this atlas before them, and they just signed their name right under his.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, the Moss connection is genuinely spooky, I'll give you that, but — and here's the thing — what's the alternative? Not take the atlas? Not sign the card? They need the map. Kadou needs it to find Joker Worlds where they can harvest magic items for the tithe. Without it, they're flying blind through nearly three million empty worlds for four and a half months. You take the deal. You sign the card. You move on.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You could sign a false name. That's the alternative. It's free, it takes zero effort, and it means a bone dragon with a magical index card doesn't have a direct link to your identity. But no. Anzu signed his real name. Rookie mistake.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: You know what, fine, the false name thing is fair, but I think you're being too hard on the moment because the atlas itself is the star here. When they get it home and start unfolding it with Kadou — two hundred feet long, Maeve. The map is two hundred feet long. It rolls through the war room, through the hallway, into the kitchen. It covers almost 2.8 million worlds. And the text on it is moving. It's being rewritten over itself in real time, like it's live-updating. That's incredible.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It is incredible. And Kadou — who is genuinely the right person for this, horizon lore is literally his thing from Alkahest Freight — he and Anzu parse out the near future. Three key destinations. First, about three days after the next tithe: a world labeled Menagerie 1.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The Menagerie! The fairy tale moving city that collects wonders from across the horizon! When Josh said that, I literally — that's the kind of world-building that makes me want to live in this campaign forever. A city that moves across worlds, gathering treasures, and it's just there on the map. Labeled. Like a bus stop. And the fact that it appears on a map at all is strange because the whole point is that it moves, so either the map knows where it's going to be, or it's there right now. That's a beautiful mystery.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It is a good mystery. And then right after, two stacked Joker spans — Hellsmith and Glacier. Fire worlds and ice worlds, adjacent, at war with each other, both producing weapons and trade goods. The party correctly identifies that those are worth visiting for magic items, and also correctly notes they might only be able to hit one, not both, given the six-second windows.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Because the Strider moves through a world every six seconds, right, so you're there and then you're gone, and you have to — it's like, you have to plan your dive, you can't just wander.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Right. So the atlas gives them a real strategic picture for the first time. Smart to study it immediately. Smart to bring Kadou in. The session has good decision-making so far, is what I'm saying, which is why I'm extra annoyed about the checkout card.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: You're going to ride that checkout card all the way to the grave, aren't you.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I will ride it until Anzu gets a clone made of him by whatever entity ends up with that index card, yes.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, moving on — before the atlas study, there's the scene with Johnny and the twins, Anouk and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Anouk and Onik.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: — right, Anouk and Onik, and this is where I think the session does something really interesting, because Johnny goes in to get his Drum of War upgraded, and then out of nowhere starts questioning them about where they were when the Prime Minister was assassinated and Raelion fell. And the twins are evasive but not in a way that feels sinister — they were on a mission for Renge, doing motorcade work, and they seem genuinely confused by the implication that they might have caused Raelion's destruction.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Johnny's trying to untangle whatever Aut told him, and Aut — whatever Aut is — deals in half-truths and misdirection by design. The twins even say, essentially, anything Aut wants you to know is probably not something you should give much thought to. That's not evasion, that's genuine advice from people who know the pattern.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But here's the read I had on it — and I'll defend this — the twins are clearly loyal to Renge first and the coalition second. They say as much during the Ring of Truth ceremony later. And Johnny sensing that tension and trying to feel out where they stand — I think that's good instincts from a character who's supposed to be a spy network operative.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The instincts are fine. The execution is a mess. He rolls a 21 perception to sense motive and gets nothing useful, then just drops it. And then he immediately goes into the group chat — the group chat the Machine God can hear, by the way — and says, hey, I didn't tell them about the Machine God. Which is smart, keeping that secret. But the twins already told him they're bound to someone else first. The Ring of Truth is where that really pays off, though.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the Ring of Truth. This is the scene. This is the scene of the night, in my opinion, because Argyle sets up this three-tenet pledge — protect the coalition, don't harm anyone in it, no other allegiances that supersede it — and it's simultaneously the smartest and most uncomfortable thing they've done. Because on paper it works. The Alkahest Freight people pass cleanly. Salvado passes cleanly. But the two Solari lackeys? They won't swear to protect the coalition with their lives. The bell doesn't ding. They're lying. They'll run if things go south.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is — and I'll give Argyle credit here — that's exactly the kind of information you want from a Ring of Truth. You're not trying to make cowards into heroes. You're trying to know who your cowards are. And now they know. The two pencil-pushers from Solari Sub-surface won't die for the cause. That's fine. That's actionable intelligence. You put them behind a wall, not in front of one.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Exactly! And then Argyle asks the follow-up — would you sell the group out to another group? And they say no, and the bell dings, they're telling the truth. So they're not traitors, they're just — they're just scared. They're normal people who are scared. And I think that's a really human moment in the middle of all this cosmic strider stuff.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
