transcript.text: Agreed. The twins, though. That's where it gets uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The twins won't promise not to harm coalition members, won't promise no outside allegiances, and they basically tell Argyle to his face — if Renge tells us to abandon you all and join someone else, we will do so. We are hers before we are yours. That's a — I mean, that's a big thing to hear under a truth compulsion.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Argyle's response is interesting. He doesn't kick them out. He says, I would never abandon my allies, the Judge sent me here specifically, and then he kind of — he pivots to, well, you have access to the workshop and gunpowder, so you're incentivized to stay. Which is a pragmatic move but also a slightly desperate one. He's basically saying, I can't make you loyal, so here are the material reasons it makes sense to stick around.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which I think is the right play! What else are you going to do? Kick out your best tinkerers because they have a prior commitment? That prior commitment is to Renge, who, from what we know, is not actively hostile to the coalition. The twins even say they don't believe Renge would actually do that. They're just being honest about the hierarchy of their loyalties.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think the honesty is what saves it. If they'd lied and the bell had caught them, that's a different conversation. But they stood there and told the truth, which means at minimum they're operating in good faith about the limits of their loyalty. I can work with someone who tells me where their line is. I can't work with someone who pretends they don't have one.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Beautifully said, actually. See, you can be warm when you want to be.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Don't push it. What's next, the Radiant Arms recruitment?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The Radiant Arms recruitment! Okay, so this is where Johnny goes absolutely nuclear with the bard toolkit, and I mean that in the best way. He casts Melodious Spell to hide the verbal and somatic components of his next spell, then spends a mythic point on Perceive the Threads of Fate, then uses Shameless Request so even if he bombs the diplomacy check there's no blowback, and then layers on a mythic power surge for advantage on the roll. He is pulling out every stop. Every single one. For a diplomacy check to convince a faction of gun-toting androids to abandon their fortified base and move in with the party.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And it works. The roll is high enough. Atul — who is Y'shael's second, an android with clear synthetic skin and three firearms and an arm-mounted barrel — agrees, but he negotiates. Two rooms from future base upgrades, and a commitment to procure rare materials for their reverse engineering of the Sable and Sons laser weapon the party gave them earlier.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which is such a good deal for the party. They give up two rooms they haven't even built yet and a shopping list, and in exchange they get Radiant Arms — three combat-ready androids with a van full of guns and firearm prototypes — as permanent base defenders. Plus they get to harvest the Final Calibur heart, which is literally a cardboard box full of bullets, and that's worth thirty energy, or thirty-two with the siphon array.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The siphon array continues to be the best investment they've made. Every item they feed into the heart gets plus two, and it compounds. They're at one hundred and five energy now after the heart harvest, and they're sitting on it rather than spending, which — finally — is the correct call.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And I want to talk about the base defense debate, because this is where the party actually disagrees with each other and it's a real strategic fork. Argyle wants turrets. He sees turrets as a deterrent, as visible hard power, and his logic is, we're in a cold war state, if we start doing espionage and logistics stuff we're going to make enemies, and if we make enemies we need to be able to shoot them when they show up. Benny argues for feedback shielding — reactive damage to anyone who hits the base in melee, plus once per tithe you can negate a structural hazard, which could mean a bomb from a plane. Johnny wants the spoofing transmitter and masking matrix, the espionage route, because he says they're not at open war yet and the logistics tools pay for themselves over time.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Anzu sides with the logistics route, which is interesting because Anzu is the one who's been most worried about being a glass cannon, and you'd think he'd want the hard defenses. But his argument is sound — the sooner you invest in cost-saving infrastructure, the longer it has to compound. The masking matrix halves your tithe every three cycles. Over fifteen cycles, that's massive.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they don't end up going logistics! They end up getting alarm wards because Radiant Arms basically tells them, you don't have alarms, someone's going to sneak in and slit your throat, and also, they want a firing range. So they build the firing range, they oil the walls — which is an eight-hour ritual of just... walking around with a bucket and a mop, and I love that Josh made the secondary caster requirement mean someone has to walk around with Argyle while he slathers oil on everything —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Anouk does it. The crafting twin. She comes out with a mop. They both crit. The walls are extremely slippery.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Extremely slippery and oil-slicked and they have a moat and barbed wire with speaker alarms and gun slits for the androids and a firing range with magically conjured humanoid targets. The base is becoming a fortress. And I think Argyle's instinct was right — you need the deterrent, because the moment they recruit Radiant Arms, they've moved the line of defense. Hildebrandt's Paavo is standing right there when Johnny tells him, and his face just falls. He goes from, don't worry, Radiant Arms is between us and the Pale Lantern Society, to — oh, you moved them. Now where's our buffer?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And that's a real consequence. They made a strategic gain and created a strategic vulnerability in the same move. The Pale Lantern Society — which is an ancient organization, predating even the Gods and the Iridescent Church, formerly a cabal of necromantic warlords — now has a direct line to Hildebrandt's territory with Radiant Arms gone. And the Pale Lantern Society has a radar dish on their antenna, which Argyle correctly identifies as probably a spoofing array or parasitic hook. That's the faction that can manipulate your tithe payments.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So you think moving Radiant Arms was a mistake?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: No. I think it was the right call with a real cost. You consolidate your forces, you get three gunners defending your base, you gain thirty-two energy. But you owe Hildebrandt now, because you just made their neighborhood worse, and Paavo is the type who remembers.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Speaking of Paavo — the plane conversation! Argyle asks about the rumors that Hildebrandt's been shooting down Ternion's planes, and Paavo just — deflects. We don't make military planes. We make consumer planes. We don't equip consumer planes with guns. And Argyle literally chooses not to sense motive! He says, nope, I don't want to know, I don't care if they shoot down the other planes, as long as they're on our side. That is a choice! That is a character-defining choice!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's also a choice that's going to bite them, because Hildebrandt is shady. Ternion's Jethro already warned them about this — engineers who go to Hildebrandt disappear. And then it comes out that Verdant Holdings — the agricultural powerhouse — apparently firebombed Hildebrandt at a Halloween party. Disguised themselves, took hostages, poured acid on the floors, broke into a vault. So the neighborhood is a snake pit, and Argyle is choosing to not look at the snakes.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He's choosing to not look at the snakes because the snakes are currently pointed at other snakes, and as long as they're biting each other, he doesn't need to know which fangs are venomous. Is that naive? Maybe. Is it pragmatic? Absolutely. You can't fight every battle. You can't audit every ally. At some point you have to say, this person is useful, they're not actively trying to kill me, and I'm going to table the rest.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think that works until it doesn't, and when it doesn't, it's going to be spectacular. But let's get to the phone calls, because that's where the session ends and it's where some real plot seeds drop.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Yes! Three phone calls home. Argyle calls Dame Quay at the Scale, Johnny calls Red from the Ghosts of Raelion, and Benny calls Atum, his father-heart from Belvedere. And all three calls give you something different but they're all — they all plant something.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Argyle's call to Dame Quay is the most strategic. He mentions the atlas, asks for research on Coulombe Honorsworn — the founder of the Scale, whose statue they found in the Undercroft — and Dame Quay drops that the quorum, the halfway point of the Strider's journey, is where Voice of Many was found. It's also the Shackled Prince's territory. There'll be good items there, but it's dangerous.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And the Shackled Prince is — we don't know a ton, but we know it's a big deal, right, this isn't just a random encounter, this is a named power on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: We know it's firmly his territory and Dame Quay says they only held it briefly. That's a signpost for the campaign's midpoint, roughly.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Johnny's call to Red is the one that gives me chills, though. Red says there's been movement — weapons moving through back channels, people getting restless since Teller's Run blew up, everybody's tense, everybody's gearing up for something. Something big is coming on the home front and Johnny literally can't do anything about it from the Strider. He's stuck on a moving city four and a half months from home, and back home the powder keg is being loaded.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Red can't even tell him what it is, because he doesn't know. He's hearing rumblings. He's been asking Donnie, whoever Donnie is, and Donnie says wait and see. That's a thread that's going to pull tight when they get back, assuming they get back.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then Benny's call to Atum is the one that — okay, this is where I might be reading too far into it, but Atum is a heart from Belvedere, right, and when Benny mentions the Machine God, Atum's entire demeanor shifts. Josh describes his communication style as a hydrogen orbital, constantly shifting through excited states, and he gets intensely interested. He wants to know everything about the Machine God's construction. He wants Benny to extract information about how the Machine God was built, because — and this is the key — Atum is aware he was manufactured using the newer, more restrictive, shackled process. He's not quite old enough to be an old heart. And he wants to change that.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Atum wants to unshackle himself. The Machine God is an unshackled heart from Aurelia's era. That's not a casual interest — that's a being looking at a blueprint for his own liberation. And he's asking his nine-year-old son to go fetch it for him.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which is — I mean, that's a little ominous, right? But Atum is also — he's not presented as malevolent. He's curious, he's ambitious, he wants to grow. And the party has already decided the Machine God is an ally. So sharing information between allies isn't inherently dangerous.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Unless Atum's definition of unshackling himself involves consuming other hearts, which — let's be honest — is not outside the realm of possibility in this setting. Hearts eat things. The party's own heart, Eerie, literally said "I hunger" when they fed it Final Calibur. Atum is a Belvedere heart, Belvedere is an org that grew into a power by folding hearts into its hierarchy, and the Machine God just connected to the party's heart network. If Atum can access that network through his son—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: You're constructing a conspiracy theory based on a hydrogen orbital and a hungry heart.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm constructing a pattern based on how hearts in this setting actually behave. They consume. They network. They grow. And the party just linked an ancient unshackled heart into their network while Benny's father — a shackled heart who wants to be unshackled — is on the other end of a phone call asking for construction details. That's not a conspiracy theory. That's a plot Chekhov just hung on the wall.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: ...Okay. I hate that you might be right about that. But I also think you're doing the thing where you take the most ominous possible reading and treat it as the inevitable one. Atum said he'd help. He said he'd research. He gave Benny information — the names of the two Belvedere founders, Helm and Torun Karabi, brothers, astronomers. That's a gift, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's both. It can be a gift and a threat. The most dangerous people in this campaign are the ones who give you something useful right before they ask you for something that costs more than you realize.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I — yeah. I can't argue with that framing. But I also think the session ends on a note of strength, right? The party has one hundred five energy, they've got a fortified base with a moat and oil-slicked walls and alarm wards and a firing range, they've got three gun androids living with them, they've got the Void Atlas with a map of the next two weeks of journey, they've got the Machine God as a secret ally, they've got group telepathy, they know where the Menagerie is going to be, they've got leads on Hellsmith and Glacier. They're in a good position.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They're in a strong position with three people in their base who won't die for them, a pair of twins who will leave if their boss says so, a neighbor with a spoofing array who now has a direct line to an ally they just weakened, a father-heart who may be using his son to find a way to unshackle himself, and a checkout card in a magical library that has a nine-year-old runaway aristocrat's real name on it. They're strong and they're exposed in about five different directions.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: You're the most optimistic pessimist I've ever met.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm a realist. They did good work tonight. They also signed things they shouldn't have, trusted people they shouldn't trust, and called home to three people who each gave them a different flavor of ominous news. That's not pessimism. That's Tuesday on the Strider.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: ...Fair. That's fair. Although for the record, I still think the Menagerie is going to be incredible and I cannot wait to see what happens when they get there.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Assuming they survive the next tithe. And the Pale Lantern Society. And Atum. And the checkout card. And —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And you! They have to survive you and your doomscrolling!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm not the threat. I'm the one who remembers the details. Someone has to.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: ...Yeah, okay. Someone does.

episodes.title: Sleeping Giants and Sacred Hunches

A.name: Bram
A.persona: warm, boisterous, fluent but imprecise; the storyteller who relives the best moments with relish and happily embellishes. Talks in long, rolling run-on sentences that pile clause on clause; makes big sweeping claims he then has to walk back; reliably gets a name, number, or detail wrong and gets corrected (usually by Maeve); now and then runs clean out of sentence and lands on a shrug like "you... you had to be there." Drives the recap forward and overshoots

B.name: Maeve
B.persona: warm and dry, precise but pointed; the long-time regular whose knowledge of the setting is lived rather than studied. Lands the exact word, name, or date the others fumble for and reins Bram in with a flat one-line correction — she finishes her sentences and finishes them short. But she's not only the fact-checker: she needles, too, pushing on WHY the characters did what they did and making Bram defend his reads, poking at the table's heroics and at sentiment with a wink. Grounds events in how the world actually works; the only one reliably right, so let her be plainly wrong exactly once so she isn't an oracle

episodes.synopsis: After rebalancing the psychic's mind and settling debts across the Strider's surface factions, the party weighs two threats lurking deep within the machine: a dormant clan of skinwalkers tended by a dying heart called Lifeline, and a waking clan that holds Anzu's sister among its ranks. Argyle's prayers nearly shatter a hag's curse but fall one roll short, while Anzu finds an unexpected ally in the Protectorate's Yao — a believer that the Voidsong is Aurelia herself, crying out from the horizon. Choosing to strike the sleeping foe before it wakes, the party descends into a pristine, electrified hospital ward where chitinous Makers and flesh-piloted drones guard the true kin in their vats. Combat erupts amid black tentacles, silence, and calm, and the session closes mid-fight with the outcome hanging in the balance.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, but you have to start with the psychic thing, because that sets the tone for everything Anzu does this session, and I think Josh was right to do it — the class was genuinely broken, not in the fun way, and Anzu's been suffering for it for weeks.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The class wasn't broken. It was undertuned. There's a difference.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — that's literally what I said.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You said "genuinely broken," which implies it was non-functional. It was functional, it was just weaker than it should have been relative to the other casters at the table. And Josh's fix — letting him unleash psyche on round one, letting him extend it by spending health, bumping spell slots to three per level — that's a significant power jump, and I think it's worth asking whether he overcorrected.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Overcorrected? The guy could only use his class feature on rounds two and three, and then he got stupefied for his trouble. Rounds four and five he's just — he's a worse wizard. That's not undertuned, that's — that's a hostage situation. The class is holding its own mechanic hostage. And Josh saw it, he compared it to the Decay instinct barbarian, which is doing basically the same damage for free, and he was like, yeah, this is silly.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The barbarian comparison is fair. I'll give you that. The damage output on unleash psyche is comparable and the barbarian pays way less for it. But bumping spell slots to three on top of the unleash psyche changes? That's two buffs stacked. He could've done one or the other and seen where it landed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Or — and hear me out — he could've done both, because the class needed both, and also Johnny has three spell slots per level and nobody's crying about Johnny.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Johnny's a bard. Different chassis, different spell list, different — you can't just compare slot counts across classes like they're interchangeable.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And yet that's exactly what Josh did when he made the call, so — look, the point is Anzu's been limping through combat for sessions and you could feel it at the table, Tanner was — you could hear it in his voice, he loved the concept, the psychic flavor, the mind stuff, but the mechanics just weren't delivering, and this session finally gave him the tools to actually do the thing his character is supposed to do.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm not arguing against the fix. I'm saying it's a lot of fix all at once and we won't know if it's too much until we see it in real combat, which — speaking of which, we did see it, at the end.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: We did! And it was great. But before we get there — okay, so the other thing at the top of the session is the strategic decision, which I think is the most interesting debate of the night, and I want to talk about it before we get into the Yao stuff and the curse stuff, because it frames everything.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The sleeping clan versus the waking clan.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Right. So the Machine God tells them there are two groups of Herald followers left. One's dormant, sleeping, on the third floor near the surface, more powerful individually. The other's awake, sprawling, spread across multiple sections of the Strider, and that's where Anzu's sister is. Eight tengu over there, by the way — eight, which is — that's a lot of sisters.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's not eight sisters. It's eight tengu, and not all of them are necessarily connected to Anzu's sister. The Machine God said they're not all linked. But yes, the point stands: the waking clan is where the personal stakes are.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And the party chooses the sleeping clan. They go for the dormant threat first. And I think that's the right call, by the way — you strike the sleeping giant before it wakes up, you don't poke the wasp nest that's already buzzing —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But that's the thing. The sleeping clan is described as more powerful individually. You're choosing to fight the stronger enemy because you might catch them off guard. That's a gamble, not a strategy. If they wake up mid-fight, you've just picked a fight with the stronger group on their home turf.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But that's exactly why you do it now! While they're asleep, while the keepers are the only ones standing watch, while the true kin are still in their vats. You go in, you smash the vats, you kill the heart — Lifeline, the dying heart running the hospital — and you're out. The alternative is you leave a ticking time bomb behind you while you go chase the waking clan across half the Strider, and then when you come back, guess what, they're awake, and now you're fighting both.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That assumes the two clans are on a shared timer, which we don't know. The Machine God said the dormant group would activate when the Strider reaches its destination. That's months away. You had time.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Had time! You had — you're on a giant moving machine heading toward a wall on the horizon, and you "had time." That's — Maeve, that's what every horror movie character says right before the thing they left behind catches up.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm saying the urgency is manufactured. Argyle even admits it — he says "I just feel like it's stronger," and then he goes "I don't know why I would think it's stronger." That's not tactical reasoning. That's fear. And Johnny — Johnny says it feels like these encounters were designed so there's no correct choice, and honestly that's the most honest read of the whole conversation. The GM gave them two bad options and they picked the one that felt less immediately scary.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's — okay, that's a fair point about Argyle's reasoning, it was gut, it was instinct, but sometimes instinct is right. The sleeping thing is scarier. It's scarier because you don't know what it is, you don't know what it becomes when it wakes up, and the Machine God — who is not exactly an unreliable narrator here — he says "surely you can learn how to kill something that is asleep" with this incredible like — that's dripping with contempt, by the way, that line.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He also says he would have its position, meaning he'd absorb Lifeline's territory if they clear it. So he has a vested interest in sending them there. That's not corruption, necessarily, but it's not neutral advice either.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, come on, he's — the Machine God is an ancient heart from Aurelia's original party, he's been trapped down here for seven hundred years, he's not scheming for real estate. He's — if anything he's being helpful because they're doing the thing he needs done.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He's an ancient heart from Aurelia's original party who immediately, when given the chance, expanded his territory by absorbing the spider clan's domain. And now he's pointing them at another heart he could absorb. Pattern.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I — okay, that's — that's a fair pattern. I don't love that you're right about that. But I still think the tactical call is sound. You hit the sleeping target, you remove a future threat, and you give yourself one less front when things inevitably go sideways up top. Which they will, because — have you seen what's happening on the surface?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which brings us to the Yao conversation, which is where I want to spend some real time, because that scene is doing more work than anything else this session.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, absolutely. So Anzu goes to the Protectorate — finally, by the way, he didn't even know they had a phone, which is incredible, he's been on this Strider for — how long, and he hasn't called his dad, he didn't know there was a phone —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He knew. He just didn't think the phone worked across the horizon, which is a reasonable assumption given that the Strider is traveling through the void.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He could've asked.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He could have. He didn't. That's character, not ignorance. Anzu is avoidant. He ran away from his family, he's not calling his father, and the sister situation is forcing him to confront that. That's good writing.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Right, right. So he goes to the Protectorate, and first of all — the Protectorate base is gorgeous. The water feature, the zen garden, the cushions, the sand pit where Tamara is just — just destroying her own people in melee, she's unarmed, they've got weapons, and she's beating them bloody. While Yao sits on a cushion and sketches her. It's — that's such a vivid picture.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And it's very Brithwinian. The Chorath Engineering aesthetic, the function-meets-faith design philosophy. It's not just flavor, it tells you who these people are. They're a private army with a religious conviction and an interior decorator.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Yao — Yao is the scene. He's gruff, he's not chatty, but when Anzu brings up the Voidsong, he just — he opens up, and his theory is that the Voidsong is Aurelia. Not metaphorically. Literally. The true Aurelia, trapped on the horizon, singing for believers to come save her. The one in Calaria is an impostor.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Dissident Church of Brithwyn. It's a real belief. It's not Yao being eccentric — Brithwyn split from Calaria partly over the question of whether the Pontifex is a true reincarnation. Yao's faith is culturally grounded, it's not a crackpot theory he came up with alone.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And here's where I think the scene gets really interesting, because Anzu doesn't confirm or deny. He says "I can feel their urgency," he says it feels like a call for help, but he doesn't commit to it being Aurelia. And Yao is — he's fine with that. He says something like "it doesn't matter if it turns out to be the prophet of another religion, it'll still be a good deed." Which is — that's a remarkably generous theological position for a believer.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a remarkably pragmatic one. He doesn't need the Voidsong to be Aurelia. He needs it to be real, and he needs to go toward it. The theology is the motivation, not the destination. And I think that's a more sophisticated faith than what we see from the Iridescent Church back in Calaria, where the theology IS the power structure.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But here's my question — and I think this is where the real debate is — do we buy it? Is the Voidsong actually Aurelia? Because Yao has a piece of her armor, passed down mentor to student for seven hundred years, and that's — that's a real artifact. That's not a belief, that's a physical object with a provable chain of custody. And Anzu has his void paper with the imprinted Voidsong on it. If those two things resonate with each other —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You're doing the thing. You're building a case out of two data points and getting excited.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I'm — I'm theorizing!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You're theorizing with insufficient data. We have a believer's interpretation, a sacred artifact, and some void paper. We also have Cato's theory, which Yao dismisses. We have Iconoclasm, which was founded by Voidsong listeners. We have the Machine God, who was part of Aurelia the First's original party and doesn't claim to know who's singing. If the Machine God — who was literally there — doesn't say "oh yes, that's Aurelia," then why should Yao's faith be more reliable?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Because the Machine God was trapped! He was cut off, he was captured, he doesn't have full information. He even says he doesn't know if many people carry this belief. And Yao — Yao is coming from a tradition, from a culture, from seven hundred years of Dissident Church theology that specifically says the Pontifex is false. That's not one guy's hunch.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a culture's hunch. Seven hundred years of hunch. And I'll remind you — the Dissident Church also doesn't have Aurelia standing in front of them confirming anything. They believe. That's what faith is. But faith is not evidence.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And yet faith is what's driving this entire campaign. Every player character heard the Voidsong. They're all here because of it. If you dismiss Yao's belief as just faith, you have to dismiss the party's entire motivation too.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm not dismissing it. I'm saying it's unconfirmed, and the scene is more interesting if it stays unconfirmed. The moment we learn the Voidsong is definitively Aurelia, or definitively not, the question collapses. Right now it's live. And I like it live.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: ... okay. Okay, I'll give you that. The ambiguity is the point. But I want the armor scene to happen — I want Anzu to bring the void paper back to Yao's place and see if it reacts to the armor. That's a moment that's coming, and I think it's going to be huge.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Maybe. Or maybe Josh just lets you sit with it. Either way — we should talk about Argyle and the curse, because that's the other major beat before the dive, and I have feelings about it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the curse. So Argyle goes to the Scale with Benny — by the way, dragging Benny along as a bodyguard for an eight-hour ritual, and Benny just — he just sits there. For eight hours. He's a nine-year-old android sitting in a pillbox watching a guy pray.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He could've sparred with Bishop. He chose not to. That's on Benny.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So Argyle's trying to break Lance's curse. Lance is the Scale's sniper, he's been cursed by — it turns out — a coven of nighthags, which is a lot of hag. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is a success. Not a critical success. And the curse is rank five, which means a success doesn't cut it. He needed a crit.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Josh — Josh describes it beautifully, right, there's this moment where color comes back to Lance's skin, you can see it working, and then it just — slides back. The sallowness returns. It's so close. And Argyle's — he's devastated.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He's not devastated. He says "I'll be back." He's annoyed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He's devastated on the inside! And then — then he comes back the next day, he casts heroism on himself for the extra edge, he rolls again, and he gets a thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And he needed a thirty-eight.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's not cruelty. It's the rules. The counteract rank is half his level, rounded up, which is four. A rank four counteract against a rank five effect needs a critical success, and thirty-seven is a success, not a crit. The math is the math.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But the narrative — the narrative is that this curse is just out of reach. He's one level away from having the rank he needs, and you can feel it. It's so close. And Lance — Lance is just sitting there, he's been through this before, he's used to failed exorcisms, he offers to help draw the circle. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And here's my question: should Argyle have spent two days on this? He went back on day two, spent another eight hours, burned spells, burned a hero point, and got nothing. And Argyle is in a basement trying to fix one sniper's curse.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's one sniper's curse, but it's also — it's about building the Scale alliance. You go, you help, you show good faith, you demonstrate that your cleric is willing to spend sixteen hours over two days trying to heal their guy. That's investment. That's relationship capital.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Is it? Because Bishop says no when Argyle invites them to move in. They're staying put. They're keeping their territory. They don't want to be absorbed into your compound. So what did sixteen hours of praying actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It bought — okay, it bought — look, it bought goodwill, it bought — Bishop says "if things go bad, we'll drive over." That's something. That's — in a crisis, they're coming to you. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a conditional promise from an ally who won't consolidate. I'd call that something, but not much.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Fine. But the emotional read of the scene — the failed curse, the near-miss, Lance's quiet resignation — that's the payoff, and it's a great scene regardless of the strategic value. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And sometimes you spend two days on a side quest while the clock ticks. I'm not saying it's wrong. I'm saying there's a cost, and the party doesn't always acknowledge the cost.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Fair. Fair. Okay — so before the dive, we've got the research scene. Anzu's trying to figure out how to reverse the Voidsong harmony that's got his sister. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Johnny's music theory angle is clever. The Voidsong is literally a song. Looking for counter-frequencies, harmonics that could disrupt it — that's not cheese, that's applying the right lens to the problem.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And they roll well — not amazing, but well enough — and Josh tells them the truth, which is: this is not a one-day project. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is why the decision to go after the sleeping clan makes more sense than you're giving it credit for. Anzu can do five days of research while the party handles the dive. You don't have to choose between the research and the dive — you just have to accept that the research is a long-term project with no guaranteed payoff.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's — that's a real tension, right? Because Anzu's sister is in the waking clan. Every day he spends researching is a day she's still under the harmony. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Johnny's sandwich situation — did you catch that?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The sandwiches! Oh my god, so Johnny's been sending sandwiches down the elevator to Marin, the mongrel folk guy in the undercroft, right? transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Sandwich is gone, no note. Marin might be dead. And Johnny just — stops sending sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: "No more sandwiches." Just like that. He meal-prepped for a week and he's just done. It's — it's funny and it's grim at the same time.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's very Johnny. He cares just enough to send the sandwich, not enough to go check on the guy.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's not — okay, maybe. But the dive itself — let's talk about the dive. Because this is where the session goes from political maneuvering to full dungeon crawl, and the tonal shift is — it's sharp.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It should be. They've been doing surface politics for sessions. Going back into the Strider is a different mode. And Josh signals it immediately with the environment.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The cleanliness! Oh, it's so creepy. They've been walking through the Undercroft for sessions now, right? Dust, rust, oil spills, mineral deposits, steam, broken walls, mongrel folk doing maintenance. And suddenly — pristine. Spotless. Repaired walls. Working electric lights. Electricity! In a seven-hundred-year-old machine, and there's a working circuit network powering bright white lights like it's a hospital.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Because it is a hospital. The Machine God told them — it was a medical center. And the heart running it is called Lifeline. The name alone tells you what it was, and the state of the place tells you something's still maintaining it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But not maintaining it well. Lifeline is dying, or not quite sane, as the Machine God puts it. So you've got this pristine hospital with a dying heart, and it's being — it's being curated, essentially, by these skinwalkers. The keepers. The ones who maintain the true kin in their vats while they sleep.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the true kin — these are the original invaders from seven hundred years ago. The ones that came in with Herald. They're asleep, they're waiting for the Strider to reach its destination, and they're being tended. That's not a dungeon, that's a nursery.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: A nursery for body snatchers! They're — what did Josh call them — small, ropey, worm-like creatures that wear people's skin. Skinwalkers. And they pilot flesh drones, mindless beings that have minds but no souls. Neither holy nor unholy. No universal weakness. That's — that's a nightmare setup.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Anzu's occultism check confirms — these are oogathals. The same kind of skinwalkers they encountered early in the campaign. So this isn't new lore, it's a return. The party has seen these before, briefly, and now they're walking into the nest.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then the combat starts, and — okay, so the setup is: pristine hallway, double doors, button to open, they can hear something dragging on the other side. Benny opens the door, sees vats — rows of vats with the true kin floating in them, preserved. And then immediately gets hit with a fear spell, which he shakes off, and then — black tentacles. Everywhere.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Maker cast black tentacles. Which is — first of all, that's a high-level spell for something described as a chitinous crab-thing. And it targeted their fortitude DC with spell attack rolls, which is unusual. Most spells target reflex or will. Fortitude for a tentacle grapple is weird and clever.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But Josh rolls terribly. He rolls a natural one on the attack against Benny. The tentacles just — whoosh, miss. Everybody saves. It's — the tension of the moment is incredible and then it just deflates because the dice said no.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But the strategic value of the tentacles is still there even when they miss. It's area denial. The party has to go through that space to reach the Maker and the skinwalkers, and every square of it is dangerous. The miss just means they didn't get grabbed this round. Next round, it's still there.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Johnny — Johnny's play here is — okay, so Johnny does three things. First he throws silence on Benny, which is genius because the Maker is a spellcaster. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Forty-two points of damage on that bite, by the way. And a poison save. That Maker is not a joke.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No, it's — that thing hits like a truck. And then Johnny — Johnny does this incredible sequence. transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And both of them fail. One fails, one critically fails. The one that critically failed can't even react to hostile actions. It just stands there, gets squeezed by the tentacles, and takes it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Johnny's — Johnny's so proud of himself, he yells out "this is Johnny's best turn ever!" and he's right! It is! It's a — moonwalk, acrobatics, flourish calm, positioning, debuff — it's a full toolbox turn from a bard who keeps finding new ways to be useful.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But here's the thing — he's on top of a vat. A glass vat containing one of the true kin. And the skin drones can't break the vats, which the party discovers, but that doesn't mean the vats are invincible. If something bigger hits them, or if the Maker gets loose from the silence — and the silence is on Benny, so if Benny moves or goes down —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — oh, that's a really good point. The silence is on Benny, and Benny is up in the Maker's face. If Benny goes down, or if he has to move to get healed, the silence moves with him, and the Maker can start casting again. That's a ticking clock within the combat.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the Maker has already shown it can do forty-two damage in a single bite. Benny's taking persistent bleed. He got synesthesia on him at one point — clumsy three, concealed everything, concentration checks. Johnny's casting soothe on him, but that's one action per round he has to sustain, and he's also sustaining calm. He's juggling three balls, and if he drops one —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Then it all falls apart. The calm breaks, the silence moves, the Maker starts casting, and they're standing on top of glass vats full of sleeping alien invaders. That's — that's a beautiful tactical situation. It's fragile. Everything the party has built this round is fragile.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And we don't see it resolve. The session ends mid-combat. Argyle hasn't even had his full turn yet. We don't know if the vats break, we don't know if the Maker goes down, we don't know if the true kin wake up. It's a cliffhanger in the truest sense.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And — can I just say — the thing with the grub gloves. Benny, when he's hurt, he switches targets to the ugathal — the skin drone — because he knows he can hit it, and the grub gloves heal him on a hit. But the heal is random — it's three d-tens, and he needs to roll low to get a big heal, because it's — it's inverse, right, the lower you roll the more you heal? And he rolls high. Gets fourteen healing when he could've gotten — what, up to thirty? And then he takes three bleed damage at the start of his next turn and fails the recovery check. He's net negative. The mechanics are fighting him.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's Benny's problem this fight — he's built for damage, and the damage is working, but the enemies are hitting back harder than he can self-sustain, and his utility options are limited. Sixty damage on the crit against the Maker and it's still standing because it's soulless, so holy damage doesn't apply. That's — the party's usual advantage is just negated here.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Argyle — Argyle is the holy damage guy, right? He's the champion. He's got Divine Wrath, he's got holy water, he crit-killed two Oculums and an Orus back in the forsaken sector fight. But here? The enemies have no souls. They're not undead, they're not unholy. They're just — flesh. Meat puppets with minds but no divine alignment. And Argyle's whole toolkit is built around exploiting alignment.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is why the combat feels harder than the numbers suggest. The party's usual optimizations don't apply. They're fighting neutral soulless constructs in a hospital run by a dying heart, and their holy champion is just a guy with a shield.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I — okay, that's a great summary, actually. "Their holy champion is just a guy with a shield." That's — that's the whole fight in one line.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the silence strategy is clever but it's a band-aid. Benny can't keep the Maker locked down forever. Sooner or later the Maker gets a turn where Benny's not adjacent, or the silence wears off, or Benny goes down, and then it's synesthesia and mindfog and whatever else that thing can do, all at once.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But that's why you want to kill it fast. And that's why Benny's up there — he crit for sixty and it wasn't enough, but next turn he gets another shot, and Anzu's telekinetic projectile hit for thirty-eight, and Johnny's got spiritual armament going. They're grinding it down. It's — it's a race.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: A race they might lose. The session ends with multiple party members bleeding, Benny clumsy from synesthesia, Argyle's full turn still pending, and at least two skin drones still active even if the calm is holding them. And we haven't even seen what Lifeline does. The heart. The dying, half-mad heart that runs this place. If that thing wakes up or reacts to the combat —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Then it's a whole new fight on top of this one. And that's — look, I know we always say this, but next session is going to be — it's going to be a bloodbath. One way or the other.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or the calm holds, the silence holds, they grind it out, and it's fine. Not every cliffhanger ends in catastrophe.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: When has that ever been true at this table?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Fair point.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Look, the — the thing I keep coming back to is the tonal shift. You go from Yao's zen garden and water features to — to black tentacles and flesh drones and a crab thing biting a child's head off. That's — that's the Strider, right? The surface is politics and belief and alliance-building, and underneath it's just — meat and machines and old gods sleeping in glass. And the party is straddling both, and eventually they're going to have to pick which one matters more.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They won't pick. That's the whole structure of the campaign. The surface and the depths are the same problem at different scales.
