Grounds events in how the world actually works; the only one reliably right, so let her be plainly wrong exactly once so she isn't an oracle

episodes.synopsis: Fresh from their Undercroft victory, the party regroups at home to take stock of strange new spoils: a blue liquid that stores not just magical energy but information itself. Anzu's days-long research into the Sentience Distributor yields a breakthrough—an interference field that could cancel the Herald Song against the Voidsong—but it requires a living carrier of the Herald Song to complete, sending the party's thoughts toward a dangerous extraction in the mongrel-folk settlement of Tally. When the midnight tithe falls, the Strider's burden jumps sharply: Verdant Holdings has been wiped off the map, not by tithe failure but by calculated explosive sabotage. And the twins reveal that something far larger is in motion—five cosmic siblings of their patron Rengar now watch the Strider, hinting that this voyage may be the most important event in existence.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So look, the big thing everyone's going to talk about is the Verdant Holdings crater, and yeah, we'll get there, but I want to start with the Machine God stuff because I think that sets up everything that follows — Argyle pokes the bear, the bear hangs up on him, and I think that moment is more important than people realize because it tells you exactly what kind of ally they've got.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It tells you Argyle doesn't know when to stop talking. That's what it tells you.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No, no, no — okay, yes, it tells you that too, but come on, the guy's trying to think critically! He's looking at this ancient heart, right, this thing that's supposed to be this incredible asset, and he's realizing it can't remodel hallways, it can't close doors, it can't quarantine itself — it's an espionage and management system, that's it. And Argyle's reaction is the natural one, which is "why did you get jumped then?" That's a fair question!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a fair question that he asked in the most insulting possible way, to a telepathic entity, while the telepathic entity was listening. And then Johnny comes in with the used-car-salesman pitch — "hey buddy, how you doing, I believe in you" — and it's like watching someone try to flatter a mountain.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Johnny's pitch was great! Johnny's pitch was — okay, it was a little oily, but it was genuine, and the aid check was genuinely good, and the Machine God didn't shut Johnny out. The Machine God shut Argyle out. There's a difference. Argyle got the static, Argyle got cut off, and I think that's the Machine God drawing a line. He's saying "I am not your baby heart, I am not Eerie, I don't reshape reality for you, and if you can't respect that, I will stop listening."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is exactly what an espionage-and-management system would do. It controls information flow. Argyle was a noise source, so it muted him. That's not a personality conflict, that's a function.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But it IS a personality conflict, because the Machine God clearly has one — he said "the punishment is not understood unless it is experienced in its entirety." That's not a thermostat talking, that's someone who was offended and wants you to know it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Fine. He's a someone who was offended. But Argyle poking at him about whether Aurelia's armor would help — after he'd already been muted — and trying to get Anzu to relay the apology on his behalf—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That was hilarious though.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It was funny, but it was also Argyle trying to use his friends as a customer service hotline, and Anzu correctly said no. You don't hand a borrowed relic of Aurelia to a heart you've known for a week and who you just insulted, especially when the relic is on loan from Yao and the Protectorate would literally kill you if you didn't return it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I know, I know, and Anzu was right to shut that down, but I also think Argyle's instinct isn't crazy — the Machine God served Aurelia's original party, he said he'd be "very interested in acquiring" relics of his former masters, that's a thread. It's just not a thread for right now.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Agreed. Not for right now. And frankly, if the Machine God wanted to be more useful, he could start by not hanging up on the one party member who actually worships something connected to his original masters.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: See, now you're making my argument for me.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm not. I'm saying Argyle fumbled a relationship that mattered. Moving on — the blue liquid.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the blue liquid! Okay so this is — Anzu rolls absurdly high, Johnny's giving him a shoulder rub for a thirty aid, and what comes out of this identification is genuinely one of the coolest lore drops of the night, which is that this glowing blue stuff, this Mountain Dew Baja Blast—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Thank you for that image.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: —it's not just a battery. It stores information. Magic and information are the same thing at the deepest level of the universe, and this liquid is recording data, not just energy. That's what the Sable and Sun guns are running on, that's what was under Teller's Run, and Lifeline was cooking up a diluted version of it in those vats.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the reason that matters is because it connects three threads they've been pulling on separately — the weapons trade, the Undercroft operations, and now the heart systems. It's all the same substrate. The question is who designed it and what information is encoded in the concentrated versions.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Right, and Argyle immediately wants to know if they can feed it to Eerie, which — no, they can't, and I think that's the right call from Josh because you don't want this stuff anywhere near your heart until you understand it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But they're handing samples out to the twins and to Radiant Arms, and I think that's actually the smart play here. You give small amounts to your researchers, you let them poke at it, and you don't try to haul eight thousand pounds of mystery fluid up through the Undercroft in a clockwork wagon.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: About the wagon — okay, so Argyle wants to build a clockwork wagon to haul the vats, and the vats are ten feet tall and each one is a thousand gallons, which is four tons each, and there's this whole conversation about bulk and whether you can modify the wagon to fit through the hallways, and I love that the table has this moment of "we can absolutely engineer our way out of this" and Josh is just sitting there like "do you understand how heavy water is."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's the classic thing where adventurers see a big thing full of liquid and think "we should take the big thing." You don't need the vats. You need the liquid in smaller containers. Take your waterskins, take your samples, come back with better receptacles later. The vats are not going anywhere — who else is going down there?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Grayson.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Grayson is not going down there.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Grayson is absolutely going down there! Grayson's area is right below — Argyle even points it out, he says this is right above Grayson's thing! If Grayson's undead scouts find this stuff—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Then Grayson gets a diluted mystery liquid that he doesn't know how to use either. It's fine. The Machine God is expanding into that territory. He'll have eyes on it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I hope so, because that's a lot of informational battery juice just sitting there unattended. But fine, let's move on — the scouting, because Johnny's walkaround the top of the Strider is where we start seeing the board shift, and I think this is one of those sessions where the world-building does so much heavy lifting that people might miss it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a survey, not a strategy session. Johnny rolls well, he gets a snapshot of all twenty slices, and the picture is — everyone's entrenching. The Protectorate's land is growing grass and trees. The Scale's land is turning to rock. The Pale Lantern Society has paved themselves over in white concrete and built a wave made of people.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: A wave made of people! That's macabre and also incredible and also what is the Pale Lantern Society doing with a sculpture made of corpses facing outward to block the view of their base?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They're a necromantic org that also runs hospitals. The columbariums are literally art displays of preserved dead bodies. A wave of people is on brand.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's on brand but it's also defensive architecture — you can't see past it, you can't scout their base from the exterior. That's smart. And then you've got Amber Call with the reddish grass and the lightning and the Victorian manor, and the Iridescent Church has an aurora hovering above a building that's doubled in size, and Ternion Heavy is building a biplane with a slide so it can take off and come back—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is the most Ternion Heavy thing possible. They're building a little airplane on a walking city. Of course they are.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And then the one that matters: Verdant Holdings has split in two. There's an obvious schism, and the RunGunners' road has crept into Verdant's territory, and you don't know if that's friendly or hostile. That's the setup. That's the fuse.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Necrolog looks abandoned. That's two pieces on the board that are wobbling before the tithe even hits. Verdant is fractured and Necrolog is empty. So when the tithe comes and the burden jumps, you've got your suspects lined up.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Let's talk about Argyle's spiritual detour, because I think this is more interesting than people give it credit for. He goes to the Protectorate, he meditates in their garden, he starts learning about the Aurelia schism — the Brithwyn church believing that Aurelia the Sixth perverted the reincarnation cycle, that the Calarian church is covering up the fact that Aurelia didn't come back, that the true Aurelia is out on the horizon somewhere, which connects to the Voidsong.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It connects directly to what Yao told Anzu two sessions ago — that the true Aurelia is trapped on the horizon and the Voidsong is her cry for help. Argyle is being exposed to the same theology from a different angle. And the thing that's interesting is that he's a fallen celestial who doesn't even know why he fell, and he's reaching out to the Judge and getting nothing back.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Nothing! He prays, he rolls well, he gets silence. And then he starts thinking about reaching out to the Host directly, and Josh says it wouldn't burn a bridge but the Judge might not love it. That's a character at a crossroads.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or a character who's bored in downtime and casting about for meaning. I'm not sure Argyle has a theological crisis so much as he has nothing to do for three days and he's filling time.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No, I think it's real — the guy has a custode he's trying to heal who's got maybe five years left because of a nighthag curse he can't break, he's got a patron who won't answer him, and he's sitting in a garden run by people who have a compelling alternative mythology that ties into everything he's seeing on the Strider. That's not boredom, that's pressure.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Okay, I'll give you it's pressure. But I want to get to Anzu's research because that's the mechanical backbone of the whole session and I think the table undersold what he actually accomplished.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: They absolutely undersold it! Anzu spends three and a half days on this, he's got the twins and the Radiant Arms people looking over his shoulder, Salvado walks in and immediately walks out—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Of course he does, Salvado walks into a room and a tengu's jaw is splitting open with blinding light, you'd leave too.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The jaw thing! So Anzu hooks himself up to the Sentience Distributor as the anchor, right, and for a half second the whole room lights up and his beak starts to split vertically — which, by the way, if you know what Herald looks like under the glamor, that's a cleft chin that forms jagged mandibles. That's Herald imagery. Anzu is carrying both the Voidsong and something else, and when he connects to the Distributor, the something else starts to manifest.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He's carrying a hybrid version. He's got the Voidsong from his original exposure and he's got the Herald Song from whatever happened to him in the Undercroft, and the interference between them is what he's trying to isolate. That's the breakthrough — he realizes he can use the Sentience Distributor to project the delta between the two songs, essentially creating a cancellation field.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: An interference field. Like noise-canceling headphones for cosmic horror songs. That's the plan. And he rolls a natural twenty on his academia lore for a thirty-nine, which is just—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a thirty-nine. It's very high. The point is he fully writes out the plans for how to modify the Sentience Distributor. He's done. The research is complete. Except for one catch.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: You need a living reference. You need someone who's actually carrying the Herald Song to plug into the other side of the equation. Anzu's got the Voidsong side handled, but without a Herald Song carrier, the interference field can't work.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And that's what sends them to Tally. That's the whole reason the next session is about kidnapping someone from a mongrel-folk settlement. The research is brilliant and it's also useless until they take that step.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And here's where I want to push on something — Benny's plan. Benny hears "we need a Herald Song carrier" and immediately goes "okay, we grab someone, Anzu brainwashes them like he did to the bird, we turn them into a puppet, we use the rest of the awake ones." And nobody really pushes back on this except Anzu himself saying he's not sure how permanent the effect would be.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Because the bird died. The bird's personality was completely overwritten. Benny even says it — "he killed that, effectively killed the bird, just rewrote its entire sentience." And then in the next breath he's saying "we can do that with the rest of them." That's... that's a position.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's a nine-year-old android's position on prisoners of war, and it's horrifying, and it's also arguably the most pragmatic thing anyone said all night. If you can rewrite someone's brain to remove the Herald Song, that's a cure. That's a mass cure. The ethical cost is erasing who they were, but if the Herald Song has already overwritten who they were—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Then you're just overwriting an overwrite. I hear the argument. I don't think it's that clean, because Anzu's sister is one of the people carrying the Herald Song, and if the cure for her is "erase Galzu and install a new personality," that's not a rescue. That's a replacement.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And I think Anzu knows that, which is why he's hesitant. He says "I'm not sure how permanent of an effect I can have just yet." He's not saying no. He's saying not yet, and not without understanding it better. That's the right read.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think the right read is also "we should try this on someone who isn't my sister first," which is exactly what they're planning. Grab a Herald cultist from Tally, bring them back, use them as the reference for the interference field, and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which brings us to Tally. The Machine God points them there — it's a mongrel-folk settlement, a thousand to two thousand people, built around a heart called Tally who was the timekeeper for the Strider, responsible for religious rites and logging where the Strider went. And the Machine God says he fears Tally is already dead, which means the Herald cultists have taken over another heart.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And Anzu's sister is there. With three other tengu. They don't separate. So you're going into a settlement of one to two thousand mongrel folk who use ration slips as currency, who may or may not attack you on sight, to extract four tengu from a group that never splits up, in territory controlled by Herald's children.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's a grab-and-grab.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a nightmare is what it is. But let's get to the tithe first, because the timing matters.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The tithe. Okay. Midnight, the gyroscope rings align, purple energy sweeps out, takes twenty-nine energy from the heart — they're at a hundred and four, they're fine — and then the totem.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Strider's burden totem. It was at — they believed it was a constant four hundred, and it jumps to thirty-four.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: From twenty-nine to thirty-four, which means groups are gone, and Benny immediately does the math — that's two groups dead. And the party goes driving around in the middle of the night checking on everyone.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which is the right instinct. You verify your alliance is intact, and then you figure out who's missing. The skein check confirms everyone in the coalition is fine. Then they drive by the neighbors.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And Verdant Holdings is a crater.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: A crater. Not a collapsed building — Garrick Textiles collapsed when the heart died, the building fell in. This is different. This is a divot in the ground. A chunk of matter just ceased to exist. And Benny rolls a thirty-six perception — a crit — and identifies it as ordnance. Not tithe failure. Sabotage. Someone planted explosives on Verdant's heart and timed it to look like a tithe default.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And that's huge because it means someone on this Strider has the capability and the willingness to assassinate an entire faction and disguise it as natural attrition. That's a player move. That's something a faction with military intelligence and explosive expertise would do.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Like the RunGunners, whose road was already creeping into Verdant's territory. Or Ætherion Limited, who Prime Meridian publicly notes have experience with explosives. Or someone else entirely.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And keeping it off the skein initially — I think that was smart. You don't broadcast "we found evidence of a bombing" until you know who's listening, because the bomber is on the skein too.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I disagree. I think keeping it off the skein was paranoid and potentially counterproductive, because if another faction gets bombed next, you've deprived them of warning. You sent the message eventually, but you hesitated, and that hesitation could cost someone.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: They sent it the same night! They drove around, confirmed their allies, checked the crater, then broadcast. That's not hesitation, that's verification. You don't yell "fire" in a crowded theater until you've confirmed there's a fire.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: There was a crater. The fire was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The cause wasn't. Not until Benny critted. Before that, it could have been a void heart, it could have been a natural collapse, it could have been anything. You don't panic the skein with "Verdant Holdings exploded, check your hearts" until you know what you're warning them about.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Fine. But the timing of it — the sabotage happening exactly at the tithe — that's the detail that makes this scary. Someone calculated the tithe schedule, planted ordnance, and detonated at the exact moment when the death would be indistinguishable from default. That's not a hot-blooded attack. That's cold.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's very cold. And then they go to the twins.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the twins are rattled.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The twins are never rattled! Anaïs and Onik are the most composed people on the Strider, and Johnny walks in and they're mid-conversation that they immediately stop, and Johnny reads them and they're on edge, and the cover story is "we're stressed about the tithe" — which, okay, maybe, but Johnny pushes and they crack.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Johnny's diplomacy check is absurd. He rolls terribly and then rerolls into the stratosphere—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Johnny always does this! Johnny rolls garbage and then burns the reroll and comes up huge on the exact social check that matters. It's the most Noah thing at the table.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: —and they tell him. A sibling of their patron Rengar paid a visit. Not Rengar herself. One of her siblings. Specifically the one they describe as "half a man but the mountain to be overcome," the one who raises the stakes, who acts as a filter for those who are not worthy.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And they say this is the third sibling to take an interest. Three of five. And at this point they assume all five are watching.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which means this voyage — the Strider heading toward the Quorum — is not just politically significant. It's cosmically significant. The twins say it straight: they would assume all five have interest, and when Johnny says "it seems like whatever's happening might be the most important thing in existence," the twins say that is not inaccurate.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's the line of the night. "This is not inaccurate." From the people who never say anything they don't mean. That's five cosmic entities looking at the Strider and going "this one matters."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the twin — I think it's Anouk — specifically says this sibling is not one to enact immediate violence. He raises the stakes generally. So the Verdant bombing probably wasn't him, which brings us back to a mortal player.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Unless the sibling empowered someone else to do it. The twins say the more deviated from the predestined plot things get, the more empowered these entities are to act. So if the Strider is going off-script, these siblings get more authority to intervene directly.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But they also say they don't know what the predestined plot is. Nobody does. So you can't know if you're deviating from it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Which is the most terrifying part! You're being judged by entities whose rules you can't read against a script you can't see. You're in a play where you don't know the genre and the director is five different people who disagree on what the ending should be.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's a good metaphor, actually.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Thank you. I have my moments.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Don't let it go to your head. The Verdant bombing — I want to come back to this because I think the table moved past it too fast. Benny's instinct to not share on the skein, then the table checks the twins, the twins say they didn't do it—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And the twins are genuinely offended! They break their composure to say "we did not bomb Verdant Holdings, for what reason would we bomb — that is unfair." They're not just denying it, they're insulted by the implication. And then they say if Rengar told them to bomb someone, they would, but Rengar didn't. That's a really important distinction — the twins aren't free agents, they're operatives with a chain of command, and the chain of command didn't issue that order.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Which means either another faction did it on their own initiative, or one of the other siblings told someone else to do it. And if it's the latter, you're looking at cosmic-level proxy warfare on a walking city.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And the party's response is "we should go to Tally while there's chaos." Which — yes! If everyone's reeling from the tithe and the bombing, the Herald cultists are probably also distracted, and that's the window to extract someone for the interference field.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The window is good. The plan is thin. They're going into a settlement of one to two thousand mongrel folk with a currency system they don't understand, to grab four tengu who never separate, from a group of Herald cultists who the Machine God says don't stay alone in hidden areas. And their toolkit is "stack debuffs and gag someone."

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The anti-magic shackles and the gag! They still have those from — what, two sessions ago?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They have the anti-magic shackles and gag, they have Johnny's debuff stack — Dirge of Doom, Calm, Silence — and they have Anzu's brainwashing. It's a real plan, it's just a plan with a thousand ways to go wrong.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But it's the plan that follows from the research. Anzu needs a Herald Song carrier. The Herald Song carriers are in Tally. Tally is accessible. You go, you grab, you come back. It's clean if you're smart about it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's clean if the mongrel folk don't mob you, if the four tengu don't raise an alarm, if the Herald cultists don't have capabilities you haven't seen yet, and if Anzu's brainwashing actually works on a person the way it worked on a bird. Four ifs.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Four ifs that are all manageable. The Machine God can guide them through the Undercroft, they've got stealth options, they've got Johnny's social toolkit, and they've got the element of surprise because nobody expects four surface-worlders to come down into a mongrel-folk settlement in the middle of a post-tithe chaos window.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I want to believe that. I think the thing that worries me is the sister. Anzu doesn't know what she looks like.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He knows what she looks like!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He didn't! He got put on blast at the table — Josh asked him for a physical description and he couldn't give one. He didn't have a name ready. He came up with "Galzu" on the spot.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: In his defense, he did give a description eventually — black feathers, blue tips, same plumage as him, related genetically — and Josh confirmed that's consistent with what he had. And the Machine God can locate her. He's an espionage heart, he's already identified her position in Neweth around Tally. They're not going in blind.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They're going in with partial information into a hostile civilian environment. That's not blind, but it's not great either. And the emotional component — Anzu being nervous, Anzu being scared to find her — that's the thing that could derail the clean extraction. If he freezes, if he tries to talk to her first, if the Herald Song in her head makes her react badly—

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Then the plan adapts. That's what the party is for. Johnny talks, Benny grabs, Argyle shields, Anzu does the psychic work. They've got the roles.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They've got the roles on paper. In a settlement of two thousand people where the currency is ration slips and the locals might rob you or worship you or both, plans last about thirty seconds.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's what makes it fun though! That's next session. That's the whole hook. You've got the research done, you've got the target identified, you've got the cosmic stakes established, and now you've got to walk into the scariest neighborhood on the Strider and steal someone's brain.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Not steal. Borrow. They need a living reference.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Borrow someone's brain, use it as a tuning fork for an interference field that cancels out a cosmic horror song, and then ideally give it back intact. Sure. Borrow.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I want to go back to one thing before we wrap — Argyle and the Lance curse. He's tried twice, failed twice, one point short on the second attempt, and Josh says he just can't do it at his current level. He has to wait. And Lance has maybe five years left.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Five or six years. He's twenty-five, he's got a quarter of his lifespan because three nighthags are siphoning the rest. And Argyle says "I will fix this" and then he can't. That's a thread that's going to simmer.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a thread that should simmer. It's not urgent in the way the Tally extraction is urgent, but it's the kind of character debt that pays off later when Argyle levels up and can finally crack it. The question is whether Lance is still around by then.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He's around for five years. That's a long time in campaign terms. They'll get there.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They'll get there if the Strider doesn't kill them first. Which, given that five cosmic entities are watching and someone is bombing factions at midnight, is not a given.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No. No, it's not. But that's the game, right? You play the board in front of you. And right now the board says go to Tally, grab a singer, and find out if Anzu's interference field actually works. Everything else — the Verdant bombing, the siblings, Argyle's faith, Lance's curse — it's all in motion, but the next move is Tally.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The next move is Tally. And I'll be very curious to see whether they go in quiet or whether it becomes a smash-and-grab after all.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It won't be a smash-and-grab. It can't be. You're in a town of two thousand people. You start a fight in there, you're fighting the town.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: You say that like this party has never started a fight they couldn't finish.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's... okay, that's fair. But this time they know the stakes. This time they've got the prep. This time—

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: This time it's the most important thing in existence.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: This time it's the most important thing in existence, yeah. So maybe they'll be careful.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Maybe.

episodes.title: The Menhir's Last Chime

A.name: Bram
A.persona: warm, boisterous, fluent but imprecise; the storyteller who relives the best moments with relish and happily embellishes. Talks in long, rolling run-on sentences that pile clause on clause; makes big sweeping claims he then has to walk back; reliably gets a name, number, or detail wrong and gets corrected (usually by Maeve); now and then runs clean out of sentence and lands on a shrug like "you... you had to be there." Drives the recap forward and overshoots

B.name: Maeve
B.persona: warm and dry, precise but pointed; the long-time regular whose knowledge of the setting is lived rather than studied. Lands the exact word, name, or date the others fumble for and reins Bram in with a flat one-line correction — she finishes her sentences and finishes them short. But she's not only the fact-checker: she needles, too, pushing on WHY the characters did what they did and making Bram defend his reads, poking at the table's heroics and at sentiment with a wink. Grounds events in how the world actually works; the only one reliably right, so let her be plainly wrong exactly once so she isn't an oracle

episodes.synopsis: A desperate plea to the Menhir for a hero's blessing sends the party into the Black and White, where visions of trials to come are accompanied by a gift: an ornate revolver called The End and seventeen golden bullets. But when the only way home proves to be pulling the trigger on their benefactor, the consequences are immediate and catastrophic — the Strider grinds to a halt in a dead, scoured world, the Harlequins are annihilated by void eruptions, and the remaining Narrative turn their fury on the party. With a stolen Voidheart in hand and an angry god-beast on their heels, the group must reckon with the question every hero faces: was the price of the call worth the cost?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So look, I've been thinking about this all week, and I still maintain that Johnny walking out onto that stage with cardboard cutouts of the Menhir and just — just declaring himself the hero of the story is maybe the single most Johnny thing that has ever happened at our table, and I include the time he talked a mechanical heart into being his best friend with a natural twenty, because this time he wasn't rolling for diplomacy with something that could talk back, he was — he was doing performance art at god, Maeve, he was doing performance art at literal cosmic forces and it WORKED.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It worked because the dice worked. Let's not conflate a good performance check with a good plan, because those are very different things, and I think the session pretty conclusively proved that.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: See, I knew you'd go there, I knew you'd immediately go to "the dice" and I think that's — okay, yes, the rolls were extraordinary, Johnny was rolling out of his mind, but you don't roll high enough to hit a difficulty that's effectively a max-level skill check by accident. That's not just dice, that's the whole package — the crafting, Argyle's religion support, Anzu helping build the menhir replicas, the mythic point on Perceive the Threads — Johnny poured everything he had into this and it landed, and I think the reason it landed is that the Menhir recognized something genuine in it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or the Menhir recognized that these four idiots were desperate enough to be useful. Those aren't the same thing. The Menhir didn't bless them because Johnny's poetry moved a bunch of rocks. It blessed them because it was tired, because Ought had just left, and because the alternative was — what? Waiting another thousand years for someone else to show up?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's a very — that's a very cold read on what I think was a genuinely moving scene, and I want to push back on it, because the Menhir's chimes, the way they harmonized, Johnny making the connection that this was what deities sound like when they speak in their own language — that's not transactional, that's — there was something sacramental about it, and I think the visions they got, the four silhouettes in the storm with six looming figures, the cracked sun, the twelve shadows from four people — these aren't a contract, these are a calling.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: A calling that cost them a member of the Narrative. Let's — can we actually talk about the part where they killed a god?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: They didn't kill a god, they killed — okay, they killed one of the Menhir, which is — yes, a member of the Narrative, but — and here's the thing, and this is where I will die on this hill — the Menhir ASKED for it. The Menhir gave them the gun. The Menhir gave them seventeen bullets and then basically stood there going "so... how are you getting home?" The chime of mourning, the melancholy, the resonance in the bullet box — the Menhir was sad but it was — it was a willing sacrifice, it was the mentor dying so the hero could grow, and Argyle even caught that, he literally invoked the story of the Judge asking his son to go up the mountain and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Argyle invoked a story from his own religion to justify pulling the trigger on a cosmic entity. That's not the same as the cosmic entity asking to die.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But what else were they supposed to do? They tried walking away, they tried walking toward the Pharos, they tried asking nicely three times — which, by the way, they caught the Rule of Three even there — and none of it worked. The Menhir wouldn't let them leave. The bullets resonated when they asked. Everything pointed at "shoot the rock."

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Everything pointed at "something has to die for you to leave." They assumed it was the Menhir. They could have —

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Could have what? Shot themselves? They discussed that! Johnny literally offered to shoot himself in the head because he's died before and come back, and Argyle offered to take the bullet — I mean, at one point they were going to shoot the bird, which — okay, that was dark, but the point is they explored the options, and the gun was given to them BY the Menhir, so shooting the Menhir with the Menhir's own gift — that's not murder, that's — it's almost liturgical, it's a sacrament, it's —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's a god-killing gun handed to level eight characters with the instruction "figure it out." And they figured it out by shooting their benefactor. And I want to be clear — I think Argyle pulling that trigger was the right call given the information they had. What I'm pushing back on is this romantic framing of it as a noble sacrifice, because we don't actually know that's what it was. We know the Menhir was tired. We know the chimes were sad. We don't know that the Menhir chose to die. It might have just been stuck in the same bind they were.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, that's — I'll give you that, I'll give you that we can't be certain of the Menhir's intent, but Josh himself said afterward that the Menhir put all its eggs in one basket, that it saw them as a chance for real change — those are his words, essentially — and that the low d one hundred roll meant the Menhir was effectively saying "I don't know if I can continue anymore, these people have got it." That's not ambiguous, that's a being choosing to pass the torch.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And I think Josh is a generous GM who retroactively narrativizes chaos into meaning, which is his prerogative and frankly his skill, but it doesn't change what actually happened at the table, which is: four level eights panicked and shot a rock.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Four level eights who had been told "you want to be heroes, here's the hero's path," and the path involved a gun called The End and seventeen golden bullets — I mean, at some point you have to engage with the metaphor, Maeve, the gun is called The End, it came with a fixed number of bullets, the bullets aren't magic — which, by the way, Anzu caught that, and I think that's an incredible detail — the bullets are NOT magic, the gun is, the bullets are just — they're just this impossible gold material, and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The gun is called The End and it kills gods. That's not a metaphor, that's a weapon. And I think the interesting question isn't whether the Menhir wanted to die, it's whether the party understood what they were being handed. Because Johnny's immediate instinct was "Godkiller bullets?" and Argyle's was "we should probably try shooting one of us first." There's a real difference in how they processed that moment, and I think it matters.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I think Argyle offering to take the bullet was actually — okay, hear me out — I think it was the most in-character thing he's ever done, because this is a guy who's spent his whole life trying to fix the world, who has five years left on a hag's curse, who's literally a failed celestial trying to be better — of COURSE he offers to die, of course he puts the gun to his own head, because in his mind that's the heroic move, and then when they figure out it's the Menhir that has to go, HE pulls the trigger, because he's the one who's already made peace with sacrifice.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or he's the one who was most willing to kill something and live with it, which is a different quality. And I notice that Benny was the holdout on accepting the call, by the way — everyone kneeled and accepted, but Benny stood, and I don't think that was accidental.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: No, no, that's — actually, yeah, Benny's reluctance was fascinating because Benny is the one who's been questioning the whole hero framework all along, he's the one who later says "I don't think we're supposed to be worshipped, I think this accelerates the struggle," and I think —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think Benny is nine years old and standing in front of cosmic entities and has the good sense to be wary, which puts him ahead of every adult in the party.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, fair, fair — but let's move to what happened when they got back, because I think that's where the real debate is, and I want to hear your take on the Ought confrontation first, because — oh man, oh man, the Ought scene, I — that was — you had to be there, it was this incredible messy breakup where Ought is hurt that they didn't come to him, and Johnny's trying to explain "we didn't want another Raelion," and Ought just twists it into "so you want to take and not give, that's selfish," and it's like — it's like arguing with an ex, it's this completely emotional irrational guilt trip from a being that is literally a cosmic force of narrative, and I think it's the best RP Josh has done as an NPC in maybe ever.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It was a strong scene. I'll give you that. But I think Johnny fumbled it.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Fumbled it? He — what?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Johnny's argument was "we didn't come to you because you'd want something in return and we didn't want to blow up another country." Ought's counter was "sometimes heroes have to blow stuff up." And instead of engaging with that — which is actually a real philosophical tension, right, is collateral damage acceptable in pursuit of a greater good — Johnny just says "that's what people with no moral Scale do." He shuts down the argument by calling Ought immoral, which is both rude and strategically stupid when you're talking to something that can brand you with burning tattoos.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He spat on the ground after Ought left and said it was for his wife! That's — that's not shutting down the argument, that's — Johnny's wife was killed in Raelion, Ought was involved, and here's Ought basically saying "sometimes you gotta blow up a country" to the guy whose country got blown up — I think Johnny was remarkably restrained!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I'm not saying Ought was right. I'm saying Johnny wasn't arguing, he was reacting, and there's a difference. And the cost of that failed conversation was real — they lost Ought as a potential ally, they got the three-dot brand burned into them, and they went into the Menhir encounter with one fewer friend in high places. That matters.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they gained the Menhir, which is — I mean, if you're trading Ought for the Menhir plus a god-killing revolver, that's — that's a pretty good trade, honestly.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Is it? Is it a good trade when the immediate consequence is that the Strider grinds to a halt in a dead world?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Okay, now we're — yes, let's talk about the consequences, because that's where I think things get really interesting and where I actually think the party's response was — I mean, the Strider stops, they're in this scoured, dead, stripped-bare world with two dim suns, the Harlequins are just gone, replaced by void eruptions and hand creatures pouring out —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And the Voidsong is the quietest it's ever been.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Right, which is terrifying, because Anzu has been chasing that signal for a year, and now it's fading, which means they're far from where they need to be, and — but okay, here's where I want to push on you, because I think the party's response to the crisis was actually incredibly decisive and smart. They don't panic, they immediately assess — Johnny grabs the twins, they figure out the Harlequins are gone, the Machine God can't help with movement, Chuck's summon returns a desiccated corpse — and then they make the call to go grab a Voidheart.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They make the call to drive into the void eruption zone at level eight with four people and a bird, and I think that was reckless.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It was decisive! There's a difference! They had a window — they were first on the scene because they understood what happened before anyone else did, and they knew that Voidhearts are valuable, they'd used one before, and the Harlequin town was right there with multiple portals torn open. The smart play was to grab one and get out before the other factions started scrambling.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The smart play would have been to call allies. They have the Protectorate, they have the Scale, they have a whole coalition. Argyle even raises the possibility and talks himself out of it because he's worried about Grayson finding out. They chose to go alone because they didn't want to share information, and that's not decisiveness, that's paranoia.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It's — okay, it's a little paranoid, but Argyle's reasoning was sound! Grayson has already demonstrated he'll backstab allies, and if you broadcast "hey we know what happened and we're going to the Harlequin ruins," that's painting a target. They went in quiet, they got in, they got out —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Benny nearly died.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Benny nearly — okay, yes, Benny got hit hard by those void hand bolts, but he also — he grabbed the Voidheart clean! The athletics check to pull it out of the portal was — I mean, that was a natural crit, he just — he yoinked a god-organ out of a void pocket and ran with it, silenced, hasted, god-speeded, this nine-year-old android just sprinting through a dimension carrying a chitinous orb while a Quellant — which is a terrifying three-legged three-armed faceless thing that apparently used to be on the Archives of Nethys but got removed, which is its own kind of eerie — and he made it out!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He made it out unconscious, slumped over the steering wheel, and Johnny had to lunge across the passenger seat to keep the car from — well, there's no road, so I guess keep the car from just going sideways into rock, and Argyle had to pour healing into him to get him back up. That's not a clean extraction, that's barely surviving.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But they DID survive, and they came home with eighty energy worth of Voidheart, which they fed to Eerie and got the Arcane Dampener — a defensive upgrade that penalizes any non-coalition caster inside their Fane. That's huge! That's — for a base defense, that's genuinely important, and they got it because they took a risk and it paid off.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They got it because they rolled well on the identification checks. Again, I think you're attributing outcome to skill when a lot of it is dice. And I want to talk about the Quellant, because I think that creature is more significant than anyone at the table realized.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the Quellant — yes, okay, because it comes out of the void portal, it's this — it's stalking around the Voidheart, it's pacing like a guard, and when Benny grabs the heart, it pulls itself out through the portal and hits Benny with Crushing Despair — which slows him — and Josh spent a mythic point to give it an extra action to do that, which —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Josh spent a mythic point. On an NPC. To debuff a player. In a session where the players had just killed a member of the Narrative.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He had a mythic point from the recap! He earned that fair and square!

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He earned a mythic point by recapping a one-shot where he couldn't remember what happened, and then spent it to make an already-dangerous situation worse for the party. I'm not saying it was unfair. I'm saying it was pointed.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: I think — I think Josh was reacting to the table in real time, and he needed the Quellant to be a real threat to sell the danger, and it worked! The escape sequence was — you had Benny silenced and hasted and god-speeded, running a hundred and seventy feet a turn, Johnny casting Noise Blast behind them as an auditory smokescreen, Argyle throwing up a fourth-level Silence on the car so the void hands couldn't target them, Anzu re-upping Vector Screens — it was this incredible coordinated tactical retreat, and they made it out by the skin of their teeth, and I think that's exactly the kind of scene the system is built for.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: The Silence on the car was clever, I'll grant that. The second-level Silence on Benny specifically — not the area version, the targeted version — was also smart, because it meant the void hands' echo-sense couldn't detect him as a gap in sound. That was a genuine tactical insight, probably the sharpest play of the night.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And it was Argyle's call! Argyle, who — five minutes earlier had killed a god — figured out that the targeted Silence doesn't create a detectable sound-hole the way the area version does. That's — I mean, that's the kind of rules-engagement that makes Pathfinder worth playing, honestly.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It's also the kind of rules-engagement that only matters because they're using Foundry and can see the distinction between the two spell versions instantly. But that's a separate conversation we've already had.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Don't — don't restart the Foundry debate, we'll be here all night.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Fine. Let's talk about the twins' reaction, because I think that's the scene that actually reveals the most about where the campaign is going.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: Oh, the twins — the twins popping into existence and doing the Goblet of Fire — the not-French twins swivel — that was — I laughed, I genuinely laughed, because Anouk and Anaïs are these sophisticated operatives and they just completely lose it, they're walking toward the party with their arms out going "what did you do," and Johnny's standing there with "with great power comes great responsibility," and the twins are just —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: "You could have said no." That's the line that matters. "You could have said no. You go back home. You live an uneventful life." Because the twins are right.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: The twins are — okay, the twins are right in the abstract, but they're also — they're operating from a completely different framework. They serve Renge. They have a patron. The party just chose to take on a patron of their own, and the twins are upset because it changes the power dynamic, because now the party isn't just the twins' useful pawns, they're someone else's chosen.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Or the twins are upset because the Strider just stopped moving in a dead world and the Harlequins are all dead and everything is terrible and the four people responsible are standing there quoting Spider-Man at them. I think it's possible to be upset about consequences without it being a power play.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — okay, that's actually a good point, I'll give you that. The twins' panic was genuine. They were scared. They were — they literally said "this is too much responsibility," and for characters who serve a cosmic entity to say that — that carries weight.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: And then the twins cast the chronomantic shell, the temperature bubble, which I think people overlooked because of the chaos. They immediately solved the cold problem. While the party was arguing about where to hide the gun — in Anzu's sleeves, by the way, which Anzu had to point out aren't shadow sleeves, they're just sleeves — the twins were already mitigating the environmental threat.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's a really good catch, actually, because the twins' response to crisis is infrastructure and the party's response to crisis is action, and that's — that's the fundamental divide in how these groups operate, and it's going to matter going forward.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: It already matters. The party grabbed a Voidheart and got a base upgrade. The twins kept everyone from freezing to death. Both were necessary. Neither was sufficient.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: So — okay, so let's talk about the endgame, because the post-session discussion was where I think the real disagreement is, because you have the party sitting there going "we have sixteen god-killing bullets and six evil gods and four remaining members of the Narrative, that's — that's exactly enough" — and Argyle is doing the math, he's literally counting, and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He's counting wrong, by the way. He said six gods plus six evil gods plus four Narrative, and I'm not sure what the first six refers to, but the Ashen Pact is six entities, the remaining Narrative is four, and the Menhir are dead. The math doesn't actually clean up the way he wants it to.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: But the FEELING of it — the feeling that the bullets map to the threats — that's not nothing, that's — Josh gave them seventeen bullets, they spent one to kill the Menhir, they have sixteen left, and if there are six Ashen Pact members and four Narrative, that's ten, with six to spare, and I don't think that's accidental, I think the bullet count is —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: I think you're pattern-matching where there may not be a pattern. The bullets might be for the Ashen Pact. They might be for the Narrative. They might be for something we haven't seen yet. The party assuming they know the budget is exactly the kind of hubris that got them into this mess.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — okay, that's fair, but let me ask you this: was reaching out to the Menhir the right call?

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: In terms of outcome? They got a god-killing weapon, a hero's blessing, a level up, and a base upgrade. They lost Ought, killed a member of the Narrative, stranded the Strider in a dead world, annihilated the Harlequins, and painted a target on themselves for every remaining cosmic entity. I think the honest answer is: it's too early to tell.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: That's — wow, that's the most Maeve answer possible.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: But I'll say this. I think Johnny was right that they needed more power, and I think the Menhir was the right entity to approach, because unlike Ought and unlike Renge, the Menhir's whole thing is heroes. It's the one member of the Narrative that's explicitly aligned with the protagonist's journey. So the choice of whom to ask was good. The execution was a disaster, but the instinct was sound.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And I think — I think the disaster IS the story. That's what heroism looks like from the inside, it's messy and costly and you do things you can't take back and then you have to figure out what to do with the wreckage, and the party — they didn't sulk about it, they didn't — I mean, Johnny felt bad, but within ten minutes of getting back they were in a car driving toward the void, and I think that's — that's the energy of this group, that's what makes them fun to watch, is that they make a mess and then they drive into it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: They make a mess and then they drive into it. That should be on the show notes.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: It should! It should be — that's the campaign tagline at this point, honestly, because — and then the final thing, the final beat where they're talking about next steps and Argyle says "should we lure the void things to Grayson" — I mean, the fact that he even thought about that —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: Argyle suggested weaponizing the void eruption against a neighboring faction. In the same session where he killed a god. I think Argyle is having a very interesting character arc.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: He's having THE character arc! He went from "failed celestial trying to do good" to "the most dangerous person on the Strider" in one session, and I don't think he's even realized it yet. He's still framing himself as the righteous one, the one who does what's just, and meanwhile he's killing cosmic entities and contemplating biological warfare and —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: He pulled the trigger. That's the thing I keep coming back to. When everyone was hesitating, when Benny was worried, when Johnny was offering to shoot himself, when Anzu was counting Menhir — Argyle just grabbed the gun and pulled the trigger. And I think that tells you everything about who Argyle actually is versus who Argyle thinks he is.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: See, I read that completely differently — I think Argyle pulled the trigger BECAUSE he's the one who takes responsibility, because he's the one who's willing to bear the cost so the others don't have to, and that's —

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.name: Maeve
transcript.text: That's the same thing, Bram. Taking responsibility for killing a god and being the person willing to kill a god — those aren't different qualities. They're the same quality described from different angles.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.name: Bram
transcript.text: And — okay, I — that's — fine, but I think the angle matters! transcript.speaker: B

transcript.text: And whether the party can survive being stranded in a dead world with no way home, angry gods on their heels, and sixteen bullets that might or might not be enough for whatever's coming.
